Obock sits far from the capital's foreign, tourist and service infrastructure, and a visibly transgender foreigner in a small, tightly knit settlement would be conspicuous and quickly known, leaving far less anonymity than in Djibouti City and a higher likelihood of being identified or outed through community networks. Distance from the capital's oversight bodies — police complaint channels and the national human-rights commission — along with limited civil-society and rights-body presence, scarce specialist advocacy, and thin medical, consular and legal support, means practical recourse for a traveller who is discovered, detained or refused service is harder to reach and would in a small town often be handled informally. Clan and religious authority carry weight locally, and social and religious disapproval can make community hostility a plausible outcome alongside official scrutiny at security posts. There are no known local ordinances, protective exceptions or documented incidents involving trans visitors in Obock; the local record is thin, so this absence should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Tadjourah
regions.merged_summary: Tadjourah is subject to Djibouti's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is a small, remote coastal area of northern Djibouti organised around small towns on the Gulf of Tadjourah, with an overwhelmingly Muslim population living within Afar and Issa clan networks. In such tightly knit settlements anonymity is scarce: strangers are noticed, visible gender nonconformity draws comment, and information spreads quickly by word of mouth, so informal community exposure can matter more than formal legal action, and unwanted disclosure is harder to avoid than in the capital. Institutional presence is also thinner and farther away — courts, the national human-rights commission and any advocacy infrastructure sit in Djibouti City, local police capacity is limited, and complaints seldom draw swift intervention, leaving practical recourse at a distance. Limited police capacity means fewer documented enforcement actions locally, but with sparse documentation this does not demonstrate safety. Tourism along the Gulf of Tadjourah, chiefly seasonal diving and beach travel, provides modest outside contact and limited tourist infrastructure; a foreign visitor who is discreet and spending may receive some leeway. No region-specific record of official violence, of a protective local exception, or of rejection of foreign identity documents has been established for Tadjourah. Risks associated with being outed locally include friction over lodging or service, pressure to leave, and a reduced likelihood that any complaint will be handled effectively.

regions.name: Saint Andrew
regions.merged_summary: Saint Andrew is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. The parish covers the island's rural north-east coast around Marigot, Calibishie and Wesley, and holds the principal international airport at Melville Hall, so arrival, document checks and any discretionary officer questioning happen here rather than only in the capital. It is a close-knit, church-centred parish of small villages and agricultural communities with limited tourist infrastructure and thin police resourcing: a visitor read as gender-nonconforming is conspicuous to neighbours, health staff and officers, with little anonymity. Practical recourse also sits elsewhere — the nearest courts, legal aid, major medical services and any organised advocacy are in Roseau, so a problem arising here means travel and delay before help. Nothing indicates harsher local enforcement than the national picture, and no parish-level ordinance, facility rule or documented local incident is known that either adds protection or raises distinct exposure; that gap in local records should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Saint David
regions.merged_summary: Saint David is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a quiet, rural, church-centred part of the island with limited services, so anything beyond basic care requires travelling toward Roseau, and a visitor stands out in small communities. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Saint David from the national picture on tolerance, policing or services for transgender visitors — this silence is not evidence of safety, and the country-level conditions described above remain the operative baseline here.

regions.name: Saint George
regions.merged_summary: Saint George is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. The parish contains Roseau, the capital and principal urban centre, the main cruise-ship port, Canefield, and the concentration of border posts, courts, police stations, hospitals and tourism-facing businesses, including most of the island's hotels. This is where the High Court sits and where formal services are most accessible, giving a trans visitor more anonymity among foreigners and a more realistic prospect of institutional recourse than in rural parishes. The same concentration works the other way: port and border checks, hotel registration and hospital placement are more likely to surface a gender mismatch than in quieter parts of the island, and there is no local facility, documentation or healthcare protocol to fall back on. Practical friction in bathrooms, hospital wards and accommodation is the likely everyday issue, with no effective remedy on hand. Small-island visibility means that once something becomes known in Roseau it tends to travel socially through the community. Organised evangelical opposition to gay and gender-nonconforming visitors is centred in the capital, and conservative church influence is present locally, so discovery is more likely to bring stigma, gossip or indifference than a distinct local enforcement campaign. No trans-specific prosecution or visitor incident has been recorded in Saint George itself.

regions.name: Saint John
regions.merged_summary: Saint John is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. The parish sits on the north-west coast around Portsmouth, Dominica's second town and its main cruise-ship and university centre, where a steady tourist and student presence offers some cosmopolitan exposure. Local life is otherwise rural, churchgoing and conservative, and in a small island community anonymity is limited: a trans visitor who is outed may be quickly recognised across guesthouses, clinics, transport and everyday services. No Saint John-specific protection, accommodation practice, facility rule or local recourse is documented for trans visitors, and no trans-specific incident or policy is recorded for the parish — an evidence gap, not a sign of safety. There is no known local measure that softens the concerns set out at country level.

regions.name: Saint Joseph
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Saint Joseph from the national picture for a trans visitor. As local colour: Saint Joseph is a small, closely knit west-coast parish of villages where everyday visibility is high and anonymity limited. Nothing documented locally describes a trans-specific incident, rule, safeguarding practice or service; that absence of local evidence should not be read as safety, and a visitor's practical position here rests on the conditions recorded at country level.

regions.name: Saint Luke
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. Saint Luke is a small, rural, church-centred coastal parish in southwestern Dominica, taking in the fishing villages of Pointe Michel, Soufrière and Scotts Head, with the Soufrière bay area and Scotts Head offering visitor-oriented coastal and diving tourism. Daily life is close-knit, and anonymity is limited: the parish adjoins Roseau, where courts, hospitals, NGOs and tourist services are concentrated, and there is no trans-specific community or advocacy infrastructure outside the capital. There is no known parish-level law, enforcement practice, local incident or local protection that distinguishes Saint Luke from the national picture. No local evidence documents a trans-targeted prosecution, document check, facility rule or care pathway here — but that reflects how little has been recorded locally rather than any established safety, and consequence on discovery in such a small, visible setting would be societal hostility with thin recourse.

regions.name: Saint Mark
regions.merged_summary: Saint Mark is subject to Dominica's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. The parish covers the island's south-western corner around Soufrière and Scotts Head, a close-knit area of fishing villages and dive and sulphur-spring tourism where a foreign visitor is conspicuous and news travels through local networks. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Saint Mark from the national picture: no local ordinance, trans-specific incident, facility rule or parish police practice is documented. That lack of local records should not be read as evidence of safety or of easier conditions than those described at country level.

regions.name: Saint Patrick
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Saint Patrick from the national picture on legal protections, policing, documentation, facilities or trans-specific incidents. Saint Patrick is a rural southern coastal parish of small fishing and farming villages such as Soufrière and Scotts Head, with visitor-facing marine attractions, no resort strip and little anonymity in tight-knit communities. The absence of documented parish-level incidents should not be read as evidence of safety for a trans visitor.

regions.name: Saint Paul
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. Saint Paul includes Roseau, the capital and cruise-ship port, alongside rural west-coast villages. Island-wide conditions documented at country level — hostility toward people read as gay or gender-nonconforming, anti-gay-tourism rhetoric, and dismissive police responses to anti-LGBT violence — apply here, and no trans-specific prosecution, facility rule, documentation rule or healthcare record is recorded anywhere in Dominica. No local evidence was found that distinguishes Saint Paul from the national picture, so the parish follows the country-level assessment; the absence of local records should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Saint Peter
regions.merged_summary: Saint Peter is subject to Dominica's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a small, rural west-coast parish centred on Portsmouth, with tightly knit communities, strong church influence and little anonymity outside the town's tourist areas, so a trans visitor whose identity becomes known may face informal stigma or refused service, with official recourse based in Roseau far to the south. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Saint Peter from the national picture: no parish-level protection, documented local enforcement pattern, or differing facility or documentation practice is known.

regions.name: Midtjylland
regions.merged_summary: Midtjylland is subject to Denmark's national legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination regime in full, with no local exception. The region covers central Jutland, taking in Aarhus — a university city with visible LGBTQ+ venues, an annual Pride event and established community organizing — alongside smaller towns such as Herning, Holstebro, Skive and Silkeborg and a broad rural hinterland that is more socially conventional than the capital. Midtjylland also carries Denmark's second-largest tourism economy, and visitors can generally expect professional police, courts and public services. Away from Aarhus, smaller and rural communities have a less visible trans presence and fewer specialist services, where a trans visitor may more often meet staring, intrusive curiosity, misgendering or awkward friction in everyday encounters than in the regional city. No local rule, policing practice, facility limitation or documented pattern of targeting of trans visitors has been reported for Midtjylland; given how thinly local experience is documented, that reflects the limits of available regional reporting rather than confirmed safety, and the exposures that do surface tend to be social friction or bureaucratic uncertainty.

regions.name: Nordjylland
regions.merged_summary: Nordjylland operates entirely under Denmark's national legal regime, with no local exception or separate Jutlandic rules for policing, border control or custody. The region is Denmark's most rural and socially conservative, with Aalborg its only sizeable city and the rest made up of small coastal and rural communities where anonymity is low and familiarity with visibly trans visitors is thinner than in Copenhagen. In practice, a trans visitor who is outed is more likely to meet staring, curiosity, misgendering or bureaucratic confusion in services and small-town encounters than hostility: no local law, policing practice, detention rule or pattern of organised targeting of transgender visitors has been documented. Danish legal remedies, including complaints to the Board of Equal Treatment, remain fully operative here. Trans-specific healthcare is limited regionally and waiting times are long, which matters if you need continuity of care while travelling; the national rule allowing a transgender inmate to serve in a men's prison department also applies. Overall, the realistic exposure is elevated social and administrative friction rather than official hostility.

regions.name: Distrito Nacional
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Dominican Republic national law in full, with no local exception.

Distrito Nacional covers Santo Domingo and is the country's most urban, cosmopolitan and tourist-facing place. The Zona Colonial and other hotel districts are accustomed to foreign guests, the capital holds the largest LGBTQ nightlife and civil-society presence — among them Amigos Siempre Amigos and allied trans organisations, an annual Pride march, and greater urban anonymity than provincial towns — and tourism, diplomacy and private hospitals can ease lodging and emergency care. This modestly softens everyday scrutiny for a trans visitor but does not amount to local protection: public-order policing is concentrated on the capital's nightlife, and a visitor who is outed at a hotel, club, checkpoint or clinic can face intrusive questioning, refusal of service or care, extortion, harassment or violence with little practical redress. Local conditions track the national baseline closely, without a municipal layer adding safeguards or exceptions. Visitors register on their home-issued documents, and no local requirement to disclose or alter gender markers is documented, though how police respond to harassment of an outed trans visitor remains uncertain.

regions.name: Hermanas
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Dominican Republic national law in full, with no local exception.

Hermanas Mirabal is a small, largely rural province where a visibly transgender visitor may attract closer scrutiny and gossip, with fewer local support or advocacy resources to turn to. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Hermanas from the national picture — no documented local enforcement pattern, protective measure, or visitor-facing rule — and this lack of local documentation should not be read as reassurance about conditions on the ground.

regions.name: La Altagracia
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Dominican Republic national law in full, with no local exception.

La Altagracia is the country's main resort province, built around the Punta Cana–Bávaro tourism corridor — a large, foreigner-accustomed hospitality economy inside and around gated resorts. Much everyday visitor contact is with hotels, nightlife and tour services whose staff handle international guests routinely and whose business depends on smoothing over disputes rather than involving police. That transactional tolerance modestly lowers everyday outing friction and service refusal compared with inland provinces, but it is not a legal shield. Policing in the corridor is tourism-oriented, and police visibility of LGBTQ people is less prominent here than in the capital. Realistic frictions remain: document mismatches at hotel check-in, ward placement by birth sex in hospital, stares, comment or an occasional refusal of service, with limited practical recourse if a trans visitor is outed. Away from the hotel strip, rural inland areas are more conservative, and Higüey, the provincial seat, hosts the country's national Catholic pilgrimage centre, where strong Catholic and evangelical influence shapes local mores. No local ordinance, protective mechanism or documented enforcement pattern specific to the province — in either direction — was established for trans visitors.

regions.name: La Estrelleta
regions.merged_summary: La Estrelleta is subject to Dominican Republic national law in full, with no local exception. Geographically, it is a poor, rural, mountainous border province with little visitor infrastructure and frequent document and security checks. No region-specific law, enforcement pattern, protective mechanism, or documented trans-specific targeting was found that distinguishes the province from the national picture; this reflects an absence of local evidence rather than confirmed safety, so conditions on the ground should be treated as unverified rather than benign. Travellers should expect that anything documented at national level applies here unchanged.

regions.name: La Romana
regions.merged_summary: La Romana is subject to Dominican Republic national law in full, with no local exception. The province is an eastern coastal resort and cruise economy anchored by Casa de Campo, Altos de Chavón, Bayahibe and Dominicus, with a marina, a sizeable expatriate and visiting-yacht community, and large numbers of foreign guests. Within hotels, golf complexes and private developments, staff are hospitality-trained and used to varied foreign presentations, so routine interactions may go smoothly — though this is private-property discretion, not a legal safeguard, and any protection it offers is uneven and ends at the resort boundary. Away from those enclaves the province is a small, socially conservative sugar-region town shaped by Catholic and evangelical norms, where a visibly trans visitor is conspicuous and conformity pressure is stronger. Discovery is most likely at hotel check-in, a police stop, or a medical or custody encounter, where documents showing birth-sex status can prompt intrusive questioning; outcomes there range from refusal of lodging or facilities and misgendering to discretionary police harassment or extortion, with no trans-specific legal remedy locally. There is no local trans organisation or trans-specific health service, so issues such as document mismatches or hormone continuity are resolved by individual staff discretion. No documented local ordinance, protection, or incident of anti-trans policing distinguishes La Romana from the national picture; recorded police action against queer venues and Pride is dated and concentrated in the capital, and the absence of local records should not be read as an absence of risk. Outside the tourist enclaves, advocacy oversight is thin and recourse limited.

regions.name: Bejaia
regions.merged_summary: Bejaia is subject to Algeria's national law in full, with no local exception. Bejaia is a coastal city in Kabylie in Algeria's north-east, with a tourism economy and a university presence; its strong Amazigh identity and secular political currents are generally described as giving it a somewhat less conservative social climate than the interior, which may modestly soften everyday street reactions. That reputation, however, is not evidence of acceptance of transgender people, and the city is not so heavily touristed that policing or court practice differs materially from the rest of the country. No local trans organisation, sanctuary practice, protective facility, document rule or enforcement exception is documented for Bejaia, and the specific treatment of transgender visitors there is unrecorded — a gap that should not be read as reassurance. Border formalities, checkpoints, hotels, hospitals and police stops all follow state practice, and a visitor discovered or read as gender-nonconforming can be stopped, questioned, extorted or detained with little credible recourse. Family and community scrutiny can also be severe. In short, the local social climate may be somewhat milder than Algeria's interior, while legal and institutional exposure remains unchanged.

regions.name: Bouira
regions.merged_summary: Bouira is subject to Algeria's national law in full, with no local exception. The wilaya is a largely rural, socially conservative interior province of northern Algeria with limited tourist-facing infrastructure and little anonymity for outsiders. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Bouira from the national picture, so visitors should assume conditions match what is described at country level; nothing documented locally indicates lighter enforcement, protective institutions, or trans-specific recourse that would reduce those risks.

regions.name: Boumerdès
regions.merged_summary: Boumerdès is subject to Algeria's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a conservative coastal wilaya east of Algiers with a university town, mixed urban-rural character and close-knit communities where anonymity in smaller areas is limited. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Boumerdès from the national picture: there is no documented local legal exception, protective institution, policing restraint, community organisation or venue that would alter how a trans visitor is treated. Equally, the absence of local reporting on incidents or authorities' responses should not be read as safety — how often trans visitors are targeted here, and how local police would respond, is simply not established.

regions.name: Saïda
regions.merged_summary: Saïda is a small inland wilaya in western Algeria's Hauts Plateaux — a conservative, low-tourism setting with few anonymous commercial venues, and no known LGBTQ venues, trans-aware health providers, legal aid, shelter, or advocacy infrastructure. A visitor who is outed there has little place to seek help or to go unnoticed, as dense social familiarity limits anonymity and neither police nor residents are documented as likely to intervene protectively. The region is subject to Algeria's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Saïda from the national picture: there is no documented local enforcement record, protective institution, or tolerant enclave. The absence of local reports should not be read as safety — where discovery occurs, exposure is inherited from the national regime rather than locally eased.

regions.name: Tizi Ouzou
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Algeria's national law in full, with no local exception. Tizi Ouzou lies in Kabylie, where a strong Amazigh identity, a large student population and diaspora ties give public life a comparatively secular cast, though conservative village and family pressure persists locally. Beyond that, no region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Tizi Ouzou from the national picture for a trans visitor: nothing documents local differences in border screening, detention, facilities, care or legal recourse, and no local tolerance record or protective practice toward gender-nonconforming travellers is evidenced. The absence of reported local incidents should not be read as safety — where the national framework offers no protection once a traveller is discovered, a quiet record reflects missing information rather than a documented safeguard.

regions.name: Azuay
regions.merged_summary: Azuay is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is anchored by Cuenca, a UNESCO-listed Andean city with a large university population, a tourism and expatriate economy, a visible LGBT social scene with pride events and municipal inclusion efforts, and police and services accustomed to diverse visitors — a generally more moderate and cosmopolitan climate than much of rural Ecuador. Outside the city, rural highland parishes and small towns remain more socially conservative and Catholic, where visibly gender-nonconforming visitors may draw more staring, misgendering, scrutiny and service friction, with slower and less reliable recourse; everyday difficulties here are more likely to present as social friction and discreet service discretion than as official targeting. No Azuay-specific anti-trans ordinance, entry or facility restriction, or documented pattern of targeting foreign trans visitors is known, but local hostility, facility access, border treatment and complaint outcomes are not documented well enough to treat as safe. Azuay also holds Turi prison, so a stop, hospitalisation or detention hands a visitor over to the national custody pathway unchanged: local moderation offers little protection once an encounter escalates.

regions.name: Bolívar
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local legal exception. Bolívar is a small, largely rural Andean highland province centred on Guaranda, with a mostly mestizo and Indigenous population, strong Catholic and family-centred social conservatism, and very little tourism. No local ordinance, campaign or documented pattern of organised targeting against trans visitors is known, but the absence of such evidence does not establish safety. Compared with Quito or Guayaquil, the province offers little anonymity: a discovered trans visitor may stand out and meet gossip, misgendering, intrusive questioning, or friction and refusal in hotels, clinics and other services. Local health and police offices have less specialist training in gender-identity issues, and there are few trans-specific or LGBT support organisations, limited legal-aid capacity and no large concentration of specialist clinics, so practical help and redress are thinner and slower to arrive than in the major cities, with recourse often distant. Any emergency detention would fall under the national custody regime rather than a separate local practice; that regime remains the severe exposure here as elsewhere in the country. Rural conservatism and distance from services raise everyday exposure and reduce the practical remedies available to a visitor without creating a distinct Bolívar enforcement regime.

regions.name: Carchi
regions.merged_summary: Carchi falls entirely under Ecuador's national legal framework, with no local exception of its own. The province is Ecuador's far-northern Andean border strip with Colombia, centred on Tulcán and the Rumichaca crossing, largely rural and agricultural, and more socially conservative and devout than the coastal or highland urban centres. Identity documents are examined closely at the heavily staffed migration, customs and military checkpoint, so a presentation or marker mismatch is comparatively likely to be noticed and can lead to prolonged secondary questioning — though no trans-specific border targeting or adverse treatment of foreign documents is documented here. The province has little documented LGBTQ presence or tourist-facing accommodation of gender diversity: no resident trans community infrastructure, no LGBTI organisation, shelter or competent local legal aid, and no local protective ordinance to draw on. Outside the border corridor, hotels, clinics and transport operate in a conservative setting that tends to produce friction and curiosity more than organised hostility. Border-zone armed-group activity, security emergency measures and trafficking-related insecurity add to police pressure, and official practice is thinly documented, meaning remedies would depend on national channels that are recorded as slow. If a visitor is detained, there is no local practice mitigating placement in male facilities. No pattern of trans-specific violence, official hostility or effective local remedy has been recorded for Carchi itself, and no evidence of harsher enforcement than the national picture exists either.

regions.name: Cañar
regions.merged_summary: Cañar is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception. Cañar is a largely rural highland province in southern Ecuador centred on its capital Azogues, with a substantial Kichwa Cañari population, small towns such as Biblián and El Tambo, strong Catholic and evangelical influence, high rates of emigration, and tourism concentrated around the Ingapirca archaeological site. There is no LGBTQ organisation, trans-specific service or visible support network in the province; legal aid, specialist health care and sympathetic advocacy sit a long way away in Cuenca or Quito, and police, officials and medical staff outside those cities are less experienced with gender-identity matters. In tight-knit communities with little urban anonymity, a visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor stands out — in Azogues, Biblián or El Tambo more than in a large city — and being recognised as trans is more likely to bring sustained scrutiny, intrusive curiosity, family and church pressure, or uneven and refused service than organised targeting. No Cañar-specific ordinance, facility ban, police directive or documented incident involving trans visitors is known, and that absence should not be read as safety. Rural remoteness weakens recourse: if something goes wrong, help, records and specialised care are hours away. The drug-war violence affecting the coast is far less present here, but local institutions are thinner, so the national protections can be harder to claim on the ground, including if detained.

regions.name: Guayas
regions.merged_summary: Guayas is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception. Guayaquil, the country's largest city and principal port and commercial hub, has visible LGBTQ nightlife and venues, Pride events, trans-led organisations — including Silueta X, headquartered here — and tourism infrastructure that give visitors relative anonymity and everyday familiarity absent in more rural parts of the province. Against that, coastal Guayas is socially more conservative, with a strong evangelical presence, and the province's documented general insecurity — gang-linked violence, extortion and strained policing — degrades police responsiveness and the follow-through on investigations, already weak nationally for anti-LGBT deaths. The province is also where Ecuador's custodial crisis is concentrated: Penitenciaría del Litoral, the country's largest prison, was the site of the November 2021 massacre in which trans woman Helen Maldonado died while held in male prison space, and later allegations from Guayas facilities concern forced suppression of gender expression, violence targeting body implants, and inadequate health care. A visitor detained here would face that placement, and identity-document discrepancies can escalate into detention during security checks. No region-specific sanctuary, protective regime or facility restriction is documented for trans visitors beyond the national picture; local conditions combine real community resources with concentrated custodial and street-violence exposure.

regions.name: Imbabura
regions.merged_summary: Imbabura is Ecuador's northern highlands province, centred on Ibarra, the Otavalo market towns, Cotacachi and the Cuicocha lake area, and is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception. Its visitor economy is well established: Otavalo's market and Cotacachi's LGBTQ-friendly expat and tourism niche mean many service providers are accustomed to foreigners, which modestly eases everyday exposure for a trans traveller. Violent crime is lower than in coastal provinces, and the armed-conflict violence reported nationally is concentrated in other provinces and not documented here. Against that, the province is socially conservative, particularly in rural and indigenous-community settings shaped by Catholic and evangelical influence and by a small visible trans community. A visitor read as trans can expect curiosity, staring, misgendering and occasional service friction — more personal in smaller towns than in Quito — with informal remedies, thin recourse for harassment, and somewhat higher bureaucratic friction given weaker local institutional capacity. There is no known local criminalisation of gender expression or facility ban, but neither is there any documented province-specific protective ordinance, enforcement practice or facility policy, and no record of police targeting of trans visitors; such absent records should not be read as a safeguard.

regions.name: Loja
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception.

Loja is a southern highland city and province — a quiet Andean university town and regional service centre with a strongly Catholic and evangelical social character, a large emigrant diaspora, and modest tourism. Several independent checks found no Loja-specific trans-targeted enforcement, hostile local ordinances, visitor restrictions, or record of organised or official targeting; equally, no local protections, advocacy infrastructure, or inclusive-service record beyond the national baseline are documented, so their absence should not be read as proof of safety. Being openly trans in a small city where anonymity is limited raises everyday outing friction relative to Quito or Guayaquil: an outed visitor may face more visible discomfort, misgendering, questioning, possible refusal of service, and family or neighbourhood pressure, and relies more on individual discretion than on local institutions. Public institutions remain generally accessible, though local sensitivity and enforcement may be uneven, and families travelling with a gender-nonconforming child may meet additional suspicion. Violent-crime pressure is lower than in coastal cities. Local conditions inherit national custody and policing systems, so an incident leading to arrest or hospitalisation sharply increases exposure; no region-specific evidence of organised or official targeting was identified.

regions.name: Morona Santiago
regions.merged_summary:
Morona Santiago is subject to Ecuador's national legal framework in full, with no local exception or additional provincial restriction known.

The province is a remote, sparsely populated Amazon region in the country's southeast, centred on Macas, with dispersed Shuar and Achuar communities and a predominantly Indigenous, rural, church-influenced social fabric. Outside Macas, police, court and prosecutorial presence is thinner than in the highland and coastal cities, and hospitals, legal aid and trans-specific support are scarce; the main towns and tourist routes have basic services, while remote cantons have limited police and health capacity, customary authority in Indigenous territories, and fewer accessible avenues for complaint. A trans visitor who is outed is more conspicuous here, with less anonymity than in Quito or Guayaquil and slower, more distant recourse if something goes wrong — the principal local exposure is stigma, small-town visibility and service friction rather than any distinct regional penalty. No province-level anti-trans rule, locally directed targeting, or protective local practice has been documented. Parts of the province have also seen mining-related and armed-group insecurity that raises general risk. Detention here would place a visitor in the national custodial system rather than any local facility.

regions.name: Pichincha
regions.merged_summary: Pichincha operates entirely under Ecuador's national legal framework, with no local exception. The province is a highland territory centred on Quito, the capital, and its conditions differ noticeably from much of the country: Quito is the most cosmopolitan and tourist-facing city in Ecuador, with a visible LGBTQ scene, longstanding trans and LGBTI organisations, pride marches, and denser specialist legal, health and social services than elsewhere, alongside a metropolitan anti-discrimination ordinance and municipal equality initiatives. Everyday encounters in the capital are generally more accustomed to gender diversity than in rural areas, though Catholic and machista conservatism persist and street-level discrimination, misgendering and refusal of service still occur. Police handling is uneven and, amid the country's security crisis, protection is strained and investigations of violence inconsistent; urban street crime remains a consideration. Rural Pichincha and the peripheral parishes sit closer to the national picture than the capital centre, while the province is less directly exposed to the armed conflict affecting coastal and border provinces. The most consequential local exposure is custody: Quito's El Encuentro maximum-security facility operates under the national prison regime, where a trans woman died in state custody in 2026, and discovery followed by detention remains a serious risk that local community support does not remove. Local services and civil society may ease routine travel but create no independent protective regime. No region-specific evidence documents routine targeting of trans visitors in Pichincha, nor any reliable local remedy for them.

regions.name: Tungurahua
regions.merged_summary: Tungurahua is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception, and no province-specific legislation, police directive or documented local incident adds a regional restriction or protection beyond that framework. The province is a small Andean highland area whose capital, Ambato, is a conservative, heavily Catholic and evangelical commercial city, alongside smaller traditional towns such as Pelileo and rural Andean and Indigenous communities. A visibly trans visitor there draws close scrutiny and more attention than in Quito or Guayaquil, with fewer LGBT community resources and no region-specific protective services, while rapid small-community word-of-mouth raises outing exposure. An outed traveler is more likely to face intrusive questioning, social hostility or accommodation refusal than in larger, rights-active cities, and seeking police, clinic or emergency help may bring added friction, since local institutions have thin specialized capacity for this and recent official human-rights reporting for the area is sparse. By contrast, the canton of Baños de Agua Santa is an established international backpacker and tourism hub with a visibly welcoming, visitor-oriented economy and greater foreigner familiarity — but that tolerance is social rather than legal and carries no documented local protections. Any violence risk if outed tracks the national pattern rather than any documented local hostile regime; no province-specific violence data, facility bans or data on visitor care access were found, and uncertainty about local police, hotel or clinic practices is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Zamora Chinchipe
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception. Zamora Chinchipe is a sparsely populated Amazonian province in the southeast, centred on Zamora with smaller settlements such as Yantzaza and Gualaquiza, shaped by mining and border communities, Shuar and Catholic-majority populations, and tourism in its protected areas. Socially it is conservative and close-knit: low anonymity means an outed trans visitor may face persistent gossip, service refusal or harassment, while trans-aware public services, specialist health care, LGBT organisations and legal aid are scarce, with such support concentrated in Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca. Police and prosecutorial response is distant and stretched amid national insecurity, armed-group pressure in border and mining areas adds to the thinness of local institutions, and police and health-provider training is uneven. No province-specific restriction, organised targeting or documented local incident against trans visitors is known; equally, no local protective measures, dedicated services or complaints infrastructure are documented, and the absence of reported incidents reflects limited reporting rather than evidence of safety. Practical recourse after harassment, denial of care or custody would be harder to reach than in major cities, and any detention would follow national custody rules with no documented local protective practice.

regions.name: Asyut Governorate
regions.merged_summary: Asyut Governorate lies in Upper Egypt and is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. Local conditions shape how that regime is experienced: Asyut is largely rural, socially and religiously conservative, with dense kin and religious networks, stronger community-level policing of gender norms, and historically strong Islamist-leaning sentiment. There is little visible queer civil society, few cosmopolitan buffers, and far less international tourism than in Cairo, Alexandria or the Red Sea resorts — so a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor stands out, anonymity is harder to find, and outsiders have few visitor-facing support options. Discovery by neighbours or family acquaintances is more likely to carry social and honour-based hostility on top of state action, and local officials are more likely to defer to moral accusations; healthcare and police interactions may be less reliable, and reporting to police is more likely to worsen a situation than resolve it. Legal and advocacy resources that sometimes intervene in the capital are largely absent here, leaving weaker institutional recourse. No Asyut-specific safe exception, documented local protective arrangement, or recorded local campaign against trans visitors has been identified, and the absence of local records is not evidence of safety — where local conditions differ from the national picture, they generally reduce anonymity and remedy rather than increase them.

regions.name: Red Sea Governorate
regions.merged_summary: The Red Sea Governorate is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. Locally it is a coastal, resort-oriented region — Hurghada, El Gouna, Safaga, Marsa Alam and Quseir — whose economy depends heavily on foreign tourism, with large resort compounds, private security, a tourism police presence and a steady flow of foreign visitors and expatriates. Public norms there are more relaxed and street-level scrutiny of foreigners lighter than in Cairo or rural Upper Egypt, and hotel staff may exercise pragmatic discretion, giving a trans visitor somewhat more social room in everyday settings. That shielding is informal: ID checks, hotel registration and the state's enforcement powers apply throughout the governorate, and discovery of a trans visitor can escalate from a refused stay, extortion or administrative harassment to detention or forced departure rather than mere social discomfort. The desert interior and Bedouin areas remain more socially conservative and offer no added protection, and remote settings can intensify vulnerability rather than lessen it. No documentation of a trans-targeted pattern distinct from the national record, and no local protective practice, is known — an evidentiary gap that should not be read as safety. Local social responses and the treatment of travelling minors remain uncertain.

regions.name: Sohag Governorate
regions.merged_summary: Sohag Governorate is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. This is a largely rural governorate in deep Upper Egypt, marked by strong clan, family and religious authority and a more socially conservative, less cosmopolitan setting than Cairo or Alexandria, with little anonymous urban space — a visibly gender-nonconforming outsider in small, close-knit communities tends to attract intense attention, and any discovery is likely to reach police and community networks quickly, where honour and religious norms can escalate hostility. Foreign visitors come mainly for the Abydos archaeology sites and the Coptic monasteries, and the governorate has few hotels, no queer community infrastructure or tolerant nightlife sphere, and far thinner NGO monitoring, legal aid, press coverage and English-language advocacy channels than the capital or the Red Sea resorts. An outed trans visitor therefore faces the national exposure with fewer buffers, weaker external scrutiny and less informal protection, and recourse after detention, eviction or assault is harder to reach. No local protective machinery, support organisation or enforcement exception is documented here, and region-specific incidents involving trans visitors are also undocumented — that thin record reflects uncertainty rather than safety.

regions.name: South Sinai Governorate
regions.merged_summary: South Sinai is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate's character is set by its Red Sea resort corridor — Sharm el-Sheikh, Dahab and Nuweiba — where the hospitality sector is built on international visitors, English-speaking tourist services are routine, and a visitor's presentation is often read simply as foreign. In Dahab especially, the dive and backpacker communities have an informal culture of tolerance toward diverse presentation, and visible harassment of tourists may be discouraged; resort hotels are accustomed to foreign guests and street-level friction inside them is comparatively low. This eases everyday encounters and lowers the probability of discovery relative to Cairo, but it is a social condition rather than a legal protection: nothing local suspends or softens what follows an outed or stopped visitor. Security is dense and highly visible, with military and police checkpoints along coastal roads, at airports, and at ferry and border crossings, routine identity checks, and hotels registering guest documents with security. Outside the resort strips, the Bedouin interior and non-tourist towns are socially conservative, and there are no local protective institutions or legal aid. Discovery at a checkpoint, hotel or police encounter therefore hands the visitor straight to national enforcement, custody and removal powers, and state discretion around tourists can tighten at any time.

regions.name: Anseba Region
regions.merged_summary: Anseba Region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. Local colour is limited: it is a largely rural, socially conservative highland area centred on Keren, with a small foreign-visitor presence. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Anseba from the national picture in enforcement, legal exposure, or conditions for a trans visitor — nothing documents local protective mechanisms, local targeting practice, or any divergence in how the national regime plays out here. Country-level guidance should be read as applying here without modification, and the absence of local reporting treated as missing information rather than an indication of safety.

regions.name: Debub Region
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. Debub is a largely rural highland province of small towns centred on Mendefera, with strong Orthodox and Muslim community norms, fewer tourist facilities and foreign residents than the capital, and sparser medical and legal services. Much of the documented enforcement record — the expulsions of foreign teachers and hotel workers and the arrest transferred to the Adi Abeyto facility — comes from the capital area. Across the heavily militarised interior, internal travel permits, checkpoints and ID checks are routine, so a trans visitor's identity can be examined at transit points or during accommodation registration, with the matter escalating in the hands of local officials whose discretion has no working accountability. Community-level scrutiny is tighter and anonymity harder than in the capital, and no LGBTQ community infrastructure, protective institution or documented tolerance exists locally to offset that exposure. No region-specific mitigation is known, and the absence of local reports reflects censorship rather than any demonstrated safety.

regions.name: Gash-Barka Region
regions.merged_summary: The region falls under Eritrea's national regime on sexual orientation and gender identity in full, with no local exception. Gash-Barka is a remote western lowland border area of small rural towns, checkpoints and internal movement permits, where document checks are routine and few foreigners live. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this region from the national picture: no local protection, documented tolerance, or local incident record exists. Where nothing is reported locally, this reflects censorship and thin record-keeping rather than safety, and a visitor should assume the national regime applies in full, with fewer nearby diplomatic, legal or advocacy resources than in the capital.

regions.name: Maekel Region
regions.merged_summary: Maekel Region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. The region contains Asmara, the capital, and with it the country's police, courts, prisons, immigration offices and foreign missions — the densest concentration of checkpoints, document checks and security scrutiny anywhere in Eritrea, in an urban, comparatively cosmopolitan city with a high density of foreign residents. Every traveller-facing enforcement action in the country's record occurred here, making Maekel the enforcement geography of the regime rather than a lighter periphery. Asmara's tourism profile, international presence and proximity to embassies provide no documented local shield: public spaces are conservative and closely observed, and the larger foreign population appears to raise official scrutiny rather than reduce it. No local trans community, sanctuary practice, protective policing or tolerant tourist economy is known to operate on behalf of trans visitors, and there is no region-specific record of tolerance or relief. The incidents documented in the capital are dated, and no trans-specific or more recent local case is recorded — but the absence of newer cases does not indicate safety. A trans visitor who is outed here faces police questioning, confinement, mistreatment in custody, prosecution or deportation, with consular access and legal remedy largely illusory; local conditions reinforce rather than soften the national picture.

regions.name: Northen Red Sea Region
regions.merged_summary: The Northern Red Sea Region, a coastal area centred on the port of Massawa and the Dahlak islands, falls entirely under Eritrea's national regime, with no local exception or separate provision for transgender visitors. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this area from the national picture for trans travellers: nothing local records a tolerance record, protective enforcement, community organisation or complaint route that would offset national conditions. In practice, the region's socially conservative coastal setting, port transit and document checks, and visible security presence mean that gender-nonconforming presentation may attract greater scrutiny rather than less, with little reliable local recourse should difficulties arise.

regions.name: Southern Red Sea Region
regions.merged_summary: The Southern Red Sea Region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a remote, sparsely populated lowland port area centred on Assab, with a visible security presence near the coast and borders, mandatory travel permits for foreigners, and thin civilian, legal and medical infrastructure far from the capital. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this region from the national picture for a transgender visitor, so the practical conditions described at country level are what applies here — and nothing suggests they are locally relaxed. Visitors should not read the lack of local reporting as an indication of safety, and the distance from Asmara means lawyers, consular help and medical support are harder to reach if problems arise.

regions.name: Ida-Viru maakond
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Estonia's national law in full, with no local exception. Ida-Viru is Estonia's most heavily Russian-speaking and post-industrial county, centred on Narva, Kohtla-Järve and Sillamäe, where public attitudes toward gender and sexuality are generally more conservative than in Tallinn and Russian-language media carry more weight. Most LGBTI community infrastructure, specialist support and language services are concentrated in the capital, so help-seeking from here is less immediate; Narva's border crossing follows the same national entry rules as elsewhere in Estonia. For a trans visitor, the practical difference from the national picture is social rather than legal: staring, misgendering, intrusive curiosity and awkward document or service checks are more likely, particularly in smaller towns and rural areas, and Russian-language venues may be less familiar with trans identities, leaving English or Estonian-language interactions where Russian is not spoken more exposed to friction. There is no known local ordinance, pattern of police targeting, or documented trans-specific violence record distinguishing Ida-Viru from the national picture, and serious violence is treated as ordinary crime; Estonian national police, courts and anti-discrimination bodies retain full jurisdiction here. Local enforcement of protections for trans visitors has not been demonstrated on the ground, so the county's conservatism is best read as uneven local attitudes and thin support rather than documented hostility or a separate legal exposure.

regions.name: Hareri
regions.merged_summary: Harari Region, centred on the walled historic city of Harar in eastern Ethiopia, is subject to Ethiopia's national law in full, with no local exception. Harar is a small, predominantly Muslim and socially conservative city-region with a tourism-facing old town and a strong guest-hospitality tradition, which softens everyday encounters with visitors. Its tight-knit community networks and limited anonymity mean a foreigner is conspicuous, so families and neighbours function as informal enforcers and discovery or outing becomes more likely than in a large metropolis; regional religious and community norms deepen concealment pressures and the risk of family and community ostracism. No Harari-specific protective mechanism, lighter enforcement or local exception was identified, and no region-specific pattern of trans-targeting incidents has been documented either. The practical picture therefore rests on the national framework as shaped by these local conditions, with thin recourse if a trans visitor is outed — and the absence of documented local incidents should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Central Finland
regions.merged_summary: Central Finland is subject to Finland's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. The region is centred on Jyväskylä, a university city with a visible student and LGBTQ scene and mainstream healthcare, hospitality and transport infrastructure that is generally accepting of identity documents; its tourism and academic presence reduce the isolation a trans visitor might feel elsewhere. Outside Jyväskylä, smaller municipalities are more socially conservative and less anonymous, so staring, misgendering, awkward questioning or occasional public harassment are more likely than in the capital — everyday friction rather than documented hostility. No Central Finland-specific law, enforcement campaign, facility ban, border practice or custody rule targeting transgender visitors is known, and there is no local pattern of police targeting or organised hostility; recourse runs through ordinary national channels. The practical weakness is bureaucratic and care-access friction rather than legal danger: specialist trans-affirming care is delivered through nationally centralised services rather than locally, so continuity of care during a visit may be difficult to arrange. Hate-motivated incidents and barriers to trans healthcare are resident-facing background concerns and do not establish a documented risk specific to visiting trans travellers, though a travelling minor needing gender-affirming care would fall under the national restrictions and clinical recommendations.

regions.name: Kainuu
regions.merged_summary: Kainuu, a sparsely populated rural region in northeastern Finland, is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. No regional ordinance, facility rule, or documented incident targeting trans visitors was found here, and there is no known local pattern of police mistreatment or official hostility; national police and courts operate normally in the region. What differs locally is social texture rather than legal exposure: rural northeastern Finland is more socially conservative than the metropolitan south, with a smaller queer community presence, less everyday visibility, and few anonymous urban spaces, so a trans visitor who is outed in a small municipality is likelier to encounter staring, misgendering, curious questions, awkwardness, or service friction in accommodation, healthcare, or public venues than organised hostility. Practical friction is concentrated in geography — specialist trans-related care and LGBT-specific support services are concentrated outside the region, so accessing them from Kainuu means travel and waiting. Ordinary incidents are more likely to involve isolation or social discomfort than state punishment. Tourism centres such as Kajaani and Vuokatti see outside visitors routinely, and everyday exposure in these settings is generally low-key.

regions.name: Kymenlaakso
regions.merged_summary: Kymenlaakso is subject to Finland's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. The region is a small, relatively traditional south-eastern area centred on Kouvola and Kotka, with industrial port towns and dispersed services, where a visibly trans visitor may stand out more than in the capital and could meet some curiosity or unfamiliarity in clinics, transport and accommodation. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Kymenlaakso from the national picture in law, policing, facilities, access to care or reported treatment of trans visitors.

regions.name: North Karelia
regions.merged_summary: North Karelia is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is Finland's eastern border area with Russia, sparsely populated and largely rural, with Joensuu — home to a university and a hospital — as its centre; outside Joensuu communities are smaller, older and on average more religious and socially conservative than the capital region. Specialist gender services and the country's gender identity units are located elsewhere, so gender-related care and peer support are harder and slower to reach outside Joensuu, though the university and hospital setting there may offer more institutional familiarity than surrounding towns. Border crossings on the Russian frontier operate under national rules and are conducted professionally, with no region-specific document, facility or custody requirements known for visitors. No local statute, registration requirement, facility ban, state-directed targeting or documented pattern of violence against trans visitors is recorded for North Karelia. Everyday friction — staring, curiosity, awkward questions or misgendering in smaller, less diverse communities — is more plausible than hostility, and the practical risks to trans visitors are social friction, bureaucratic mismatch and service gaps rather than arrest or organized hostility. Hate-crime and bullying statistics are national figures not broken down by region, and visitor-specific border, facility and custody practices are not separately documented locally; that gap should not be read as a guarantee. Remedies run through the same national police, courts and equality bodies that function elsewhere in Finland.

regions.name: Northern Savonia
regions.merged_summary: Northern Savonia is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this region from the national picture for a trans visitor. The region is largely rural eastern Finland centred on Kuopio, and the exposure a trans visitor might notice here would be ordinary social friction — staring, misgendering or unfamiliarity with trans people in smaller towns — rather than any documented local pattern of entry refusal, facility exclusion, detention or police targeting.

regions.name: Pirkanmaa
regions.merged_summary: Pirkanmaa is subject to Finland's national framework in full, with no local legal exception. The region is anchored by Tampere, a large university and service city with a visibly active LGBT community, annual Pride events, university-linked LGBTIQ organisations and Seta-affiliated services, alongside municipal equality work; Tampere University Hospital hosts one of the country's two centralised gender identity units, so gender-affirming care sought in the region passes through that national pathway and its waiting times. Public services, transport and accommodation in Tampere generally operate without identity-based exclusion, and no region-specific facility restriction, border-document practice or documented police hostility toward trans visitors is known. Surrounding rural municipalities within Pirkanmaa are more socially conservative, and visitors there may encounter misgendering, staring or occasional friction from individual providers or communities, but this reflects ordinary social attitudes rather than regional policy. Everyday conditions in the urban core are comparatively tolerant for a trans visitor, while any adverse treatment is shaped by local attitudes and individual actors rather than any formal restriction distinguishing Pirkanmaa from the rest of Finland.

regions.name: Päijät-Häme
regions.merged_summary: Päijät-Häme is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture for a transgender visitor, and that absence reflects limited local documentation rather than a verified safety guarantee. The region is centred on Lahti, roughly an hour from Helsinki, and mixes a mid-sized city with smaller, partly rural municipalities such as Heinola, Hollola and Orimattila; compared with the capital area it has thinner trans community infrastructure and smaller service networks, so everyday curiosity, misgendering or uneven staff awareness in close-knit areas is more plausible than organised hostility.

regions.name: South Karelia
regions.merged_summary: South Karelia, Finland's south-eastern border region centred on Lappeenranta and Imatra, is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a small-city and rural area, older and less internationally exposed than Helsinki or the university cities, with smaller communities, less anonymity, and fewer LGBTQ venues or specialist services. A trans visitor is more visible here than in the capital, and everyday friction — staring, curiosity, misgendering, or unfamiliarity among local staff with trans documents and care pathways — is more plausible than in larger cities; in practice this reads as social awkwardness rather than threat. Specialist gender-affirming care is centralised outside the region, so anyone needing continuity of treatment should expect travel and waiting times, while routine services such as emergency care, hotels and transport remain generally accessible. Border crossings with Russia fall under Finnish and Schengen external controls, and document checks — including where a passport marker or name differs from presentation — are a routine feature of the crossing points rather than a trans-specific practice. No local pattern of anti-trans violence, police targeting, or official hostility has been recorded in the region, and police and courts operate as functioning institutions where complaints can be pursued, though this reflects the national picture rather than a locally verified safety guarantee. Overall, local conditions add modest unpredictability in everyday acceptance, not a distinct legal or physical exposure.

regions.name: Southern Savonia
regions.merged_summary: Southern Savonia is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception; no regional ordinance, enforcement practice or pattern of anti-trans violence is known that differs from the country-wide picture. The region is a rural, sparsely populated lake district in eastern Finland built around the small centres of Mikkeli and Savonlinna, with an older and more socially traditional population than Helsinki and a seasonal tourist economy — Savonlinna's opera period draws large crowds, and public venues, hotels and lake cruises operate under the ordinary national equality framework, with police and courts functioning normally. What differs locally is services rather than law: specialist gender care and trans-specific support networks are thin and largely centred outside the region, so a visitor needing routine or emergency treatment may meet unfamiliarity or delay, and small towns and villages offer less anonymity than the capital. In communities with less everyday experience of gender-diverse people, being recognised or outed is more likely to draw curiosity, staring, awkward misgendering or minor service friction than organised hostility, and institutions generally enforce protections. Local reactions are less documented than the national picture, so this describes an expectation rather than a guarantee.

regions.name: Tavastia Proper
regions.merged_summary: Tavastia Proper (Kanta-Häme) takes in Hämeenlinna, Riihimäki, Forssa, Lahti and the surrounding countryside — a largely small-town, semi-rural patch of southern inland Finland with a population far less diverse than the capital region. The region is subject to Finnish national law, police and courts in full, with no local exception: no local ordinance, facility restriction, checkpoint practice or documented pattern of targeting sets it apart. What differs is social texture. With fewer visible LGBTQ venues and trans community resources than Helsinki, and a more conservative everyday atmosphere, a visibly trans visitor should expect staring, intrusive curiosity, awkward misgendering in shops and services, and more noticeable friction in nightlife and accommodation settings. These are friction-level encounters rather than legal exposure, and consequences of being read as trans tend toward bureaucratic delay rather than custody; document checks proceed under ordinary Finnish administrative practice. Specialist gender-identity care is centralised, with the nearest units in Tampere and Helsinki, so locally available trans-specific support is thin.

regions.name: Uusimaa
regions.merged_summary: Uusimaa is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. The region takes in Helsinki, Espoo and Vantaa and is Finland's most urban, internationally diverse and socially liberal area, with the country's largest concentration of foreign visitors, tourism-facing services and a large foreign-resident population, so unusual presentation attracts little attention. It hosts the strongest LGBT infrastructure in the country: large pride events with official participation, openly trans residents, venues, Seta-linked support services, trans advocacy organisations and the centralised gender identity units. Helsinki-Vantaa border staff, hotels, transit and public services treat foreign documents as routine matters, including differing sex markers, with no trans-specific screening and no requirement to disclose medical history; police there are accustomed to diverse presentations, and no documented pattern of official or police targeting of trans visitors distinguishes the region. Local caveats: most reported hate-motivated incidents in Finland are concentrated in the metropolitan area, so occasional harassment or minor service friction can still occur, though police and courts act on reports. Long waits for gender-affirming care affect residents more than short-stay visitors, but continuity of care may warrant planning ahead.

regions.name: Central
regions.merged_summary: The Central Division is subject to Fiji's national legal regime in full, with no local exception, and no region-specific restriction or additional protection distinguishes it from the country as a whole. Anchored by Suva, the capital and largest city, Central is Fiji's most urbanised and internationally connected division, with an expatriate and visitor population, a diverse hospitality sector, and concentrated LGBTQ+ advocacy, health and pride-organising infrastructure that offer anonymity, practical support, and easier access to civil-society help, courts and administrative complaint routes than outer divisions. Gender-nonconforming presentation is comparatively familiar in urban, government and university settings, and the country's principal vaka sa lewa lewa community is based in Suva. Offsetting this, church conservatism remains visible across the division's towns and peri-urban areas, and distrust of police is documented in Suva itself, so disclosure is more likely to bring social hostility, service friction or harassment than state punishment, with uneven recourse. Because foreign gender markers cannot be aligned with local documents, mismatches can surface at police stops, hospitals and service counters, and the concentration of police checkpoints, churches and bureaucratic offices can make scrutiny more visible; misplacement in custody is a noted concern. Suva is also the site of the May 2018 murder of a young transgender woman — a serious local signal, though one case does not establish a rate or pattern — and there is no evidence of organised state targeting.

regions.name: Western
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Fiji's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. The Western Division is the country's principal tourism corridor, centred on Nadi International Airport and the Denarau resort zone, with Lautoka, the Coral Coast and the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands nearby; hotels, tour operators and local police here handle foreign guests daily, and no local statute, facility restriction or documented enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is known. Because Nadi is the main international gateway, a mismatch between a traveller's presentation and their home-issued passport can prompt questions at border control, though no systematic targeting of trans visitors is documented. Outside resort settings the picture is more socially conservative: Methodist, Catholic, Hindu and Muslim communities across the Lautoka and Ba sugar belt, and rural Rakiraki and interior villages, hold traditional views that can translate into misgendering, social pressure or service friction, and distrust of police discourages reporting of harassment. The documented 2018 killing of a transgender woman occurred in Suva, outside this division, and no local pattern of anti-trans violence is recorded for the West. Visitor-facing settings may soften everyday exposure, but practical safety varies between resort areas and surrounding communities.

regions.name: Centre-Val de Loire
regions.merged_summary: Centre-Val de Loire is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception. The region has no local legislation, ban or protective measure of its own: police, courts and administrative recourse run unchanged through the national system, with Orléans and Tours providing the main institutional presence and visibility. Geographically the region is largely rural and small-to-mid-sized — Orléans, Tours, Blois, Chartres and Bourges — with château and Loire Valley tourism shaping a hospitality-oriented public face in the valley towns, which marginally softens day-to-day experience. Outside Tours, trans community infrastructure and trans-affirming clinicians are thin, so practical access to support and services is limited, and provincial or rural settings may bring more misgendering and administrative scrutiny than a larger city would. The region is socially more traditional and centre-right than Île-de-France and less anonymous; a visibly trans visitor in small towns or open countryside should expect staring and curiosity rather than organised hostility. No documented local sweeps, facility rules or hostilities distinctive enough to alter the national picture were found, and the practical exposure of a trans visitor here approximates the national regime.

regions.name: Grand Est
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to France's national law in full, with no local exception. Grand Est's larger cities — Strasbourg, Nancy, Metz and Reims — are university and administrative centres with visible LGBTQ organisations, Pride events and cosmopolitan, visitor-facing settings; Strasbourg's role as host to the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights, along with heavy cross-border traffic with Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, means official and service-provider encounters there tend to be routine. The region's tourism economy, including the Alsace Christmas markets, Reims and Colmar, is accustomed to outsiders, and university hospitals are available in the main cities. Away from these centres, conditions are more socially conservative: rural Vosges, Ardennes and parts of Champagne, and the Alsace-Moselle area with its retained local law and practising Catholic milieu, are quieter and offer thinner practical recourse, so everyday exposure is greater there. Periodic security and immigration controls at the Schengen crossings, including Mulhouse–Basel and the Luxembourg, German and Belgian crossings, apply the same French document checks as elsewhere in the country. No region-specific custody, court or enforcement practice, punitive measure or organised targeting is documented for Grand Est; the local difference is one of degree, not of kind.

regions.name: Chuuk
regions.merged_summary: Chuuk operates under the Federated States of Micronesia's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Locally, Chuuk is a predominantly Christian, church-centred and socially conservative state with traditional family norms, where gender-nonconforming people may meet more stigma than in the national capital. It is a small, tightly knit island society: tourism is slight, so a visibly transgender traveller stands out, and curiosity, disapproval and family or community scrutiny are the likelier forms of friction rather than institutional action. Service and protection infrastructure is thin — police and court capacity is limited outside Weno, and formal complaint recourse on the outer islands is slight — so even protection that might nominally apply is hard to reach in practice. No documented pattern of trans-specific police targeting, custody abuse, violence, facility bans or prosecutions in Chuuk is known; that absence reflects the limited local record rather than evidence of safety, and no working local remedy for a trans visitor is documented either. The material local differences from the national picture are social conservatism and weak recourse, not documented legal exposure.

regions.name: Kosrae
regions.merged_summary: Kosrae is subject to Micronesia (FSM) national law in full, with no local exception. The island is the smallest and easternmost of the four states, with a population of roughly seven thousand, limited tourism, and thin medical, legal and transport infrastructure — distance from Pohnpei and Chuuk constrains specialist care and onward travel in an emergency. It is widely described as the most socially and religiously conservative of the FSM states, with strong church influence and conservative dress and gender norms in a tightly knit, predominantly Christian community where nearly everyone is known to everyone. A transgender or visibly gender-nonconforming visitor's identity is therefore likely to become common knowledge quickly, and documented national stigma toward LGBT people carries added visibility here. Realistic consequences are social: curiosity, disapproval, misgendering, intrusive questioning, service friction and informal social pressure, moderated by general hospitality; consequences are social friction rather than state harm. No Kosrae-specific police targeting, border practice, facility ban, trans-directed violence pattern or hostile state action has been identified, but this reflects limited local reporting rather than demonstrated safety, and formal recourse for a visitor facing service refusal or hostility is thin, with no local trans community infrastructure, specialist healthcare or trans-specific police or facility policy known.

regions.name: Yap
regions.merged_summary:
Yap is subject to Micronesia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions shape how that regime is experienced. Yap is among the most socially conservative and traditionally governed states in the federation: a population of roughly eleven thousand lives in small, tightly connected villages under customary chiefly and caste structures, with strong Catholic and Protestant church influence reinforcing conservative gender roles. A visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor is conspicuous, and anonymity is essentially unavailable — gossip travels quickly through families, hosts and local institutions. The practical exposure is therefore social rather than legal: stigma, misgendering, curiosity, community scrutiny and possible awkwardness with services, rather than arrest, custody or violence. There is no documented record of police targeting, service refusal, or anti-trans violence in Yap, and courts and police operate under the national framework, but this absence of local incidents should not be read as proof of safety, and remedies for social friction are thin. Practical support is limited: health services, lodging and facilities are modest for a remote island, and no trans-specific support infrastructure exists. Carry documents matching the name and marker on your entry passport, and expect far less privacy in village and lodging settings than in more cosmopolitan centres.

regions.name: Estuaire
regions.merged_summary:
Estuaire is subject to Gabon's national regime in full, with no local exception.

The province is Gabon's most urban, centred on Libreville — the capital and largest city — with its international airport and seaport, the country's busiest border and screening points, and large expatriate and diplomatic communities.
