Ordinary hotel, beach and nightlife settings bring routine contact with international visitors, and foreign guests generally face little identity scrutiny there; the resort economy has historically employed visibly gender-diverse people. Against that, the post-2019 casino and compound boom has left a weakly accountable, corruption-prone policing environment in which extortion of vulnerable visitors is a known pattern, and an identity or document mismatch at a stop can become a pretext for on-the-spot demands. The city has far less visible LGBT community infrastructure than Phnom Penh or Siem Reap — no Pride events, no established tolerant nightlife — so discovery tends to hinge on private hospitality staff, checkpoints or crime-adjacent settings, with fewer local advocates nearby. Conditional on discovery, the realistic outcomes are gossip, service refusal, extortion or humiliation rather than prosecution, and local recourse is thin. No local safeguard or trans-specific support service is documented, so border treatment, police responses and access to facilities remain uncertain under national conditions.

regions.name: Gilbert Islands
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kiribati's national law in full, with no local exception. The Gilbert Islands are Kiribati's main inhabited archipelago, containing South Tarawa — the capital, the most urbanised and institutionally dense area, with government offices, the main airport and the country's highest concentration of outsiders and visitors — alongside Betio and the outer atolls. Tourism is minimal, so foreign visitors stand out; South Tarawa's settlements are densely populated and close-knit, and on the outer atolls dense kin networks and strong Catholic and Kiribati Uniting Church influence mean that a discovery travels quickly through accommodation, gossip and family ties, with exposure generally sharpest away from Tarawa. Local society is conservative and church-influenced, so what a trans visitor is likeliest to meet is staring, intrusive questions, informal service friction or gossip rather than custody, and police would be likely to treat violence or extortion as a private or family matter. Kiribati's recognised gender-variant tradition, the binabinaaine, appears in dance and public life and gives some familiarity with gender variance, but its practitioners remain stigmatised, with no advocacy infrastructure, and this does not amount to documented acceptance of foreign trans people. Everyday document checks tend to follow the gender marker in the passport. No region-specific record of anti-trans violence, targeted police practice, local ordinances or local protections was found, and no recent local survey of attitudes exists — this absence is not evidence of safety, and formal recourse for a trans visitor is thin.

regions.name: Line Islands
regions.merged_summary: The Line Islands fall under Kiribati's national law in full, with no local exception. Local conditions, not local rules, shape what a trans visitor experiences: these are remote, sparsely populated eastern atolls centred on Kiritimati, far from the capital, where health and police services are thin and there are no LGBT services, advocacy groups or discreet care. Serious illness or a security incident may require evacuation to Tarawa or abroad, and avenues for complaint or outside assistance are slow. Communities are small, tightly knit and socially conservative, so a visitor recognised as transgender would be highly conspicuous, with gossip spreading quickly and privacy after disclosure very limited. On Kiritimati itself, the resort and fishing economy, along with a historic military and scientific presence, make foreign visitors familiar and the encounter with outsiders routine; the smaller atolls are quieter and closer-knit still. There is no documented local record of targeted anti-trans violence, police campaigns or enforcement of the national sexuality provisions, and no distinct local law or protective practice is known. The practical exposure is therefore social rather than custodial: curiosity, awkwardness, moral disapproval, harassment or refused service, with disputes handled informally through community pressure and essentially no local remedy. Local trans-specific evidence is nonetheless thin, so this picture rests on community conditions rather than documented local practice.

regions.name: Saint Anne Sandy Point
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. Saint Anne Sandy Point is a small, quiet, largely residential parish town on Saint Kitts's northwestern peninsula, with limited tourism infrastructure and a close-knit, socially conservative character. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes conditions here from the national picture for a trans visitor: there are no documented parish-level incidents, local officials or separate local practices affecting trans travellers, so the country-level assessment applies as written.

regions.name: Saint George Gingerland
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. Saint George Gingerland is a small, mainly rural and agricultural parish on Nevis, built around villages rather than resorts or nightlife. Its close-knit community life and the visibility of outsiders mean a gender-nonconforming or openly trans visitor is likely to be noticed, and discovery here points more toward social disapproval, humiliation or refusal of service than toward any criminal penalty — no trans-specific offence covering presentation is known locally. Practical support is thinner than on Saint Kitts: fewer lodging and medical options, sparser services, and a police response that is correspondingly less available. No parish-level protections, local ordinances or documented anti-trans incidents are recorded for Gingerland, and no organised campaign of violence is known — but the lack of a local record should not be read as a safety signal; it is the parish's conditions and small scale, rather than any local rule, that shape what a trans visitor will actually encounter.

regions.name: Saint John Capisterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint John Capisterre is a small, rural parish on northern Saint Kitts taking in Dieppe Bay, Saddler and St. Paul's, with little tourist-facing infrastructure, limited anonymity, and reaching sympathetic services or legal support typically meaning travel to Basseterre. The region is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Saint John Capisterre from the national picture for a trans visitor.

regions.name: Saint John Figtree
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. Accounts differ on the parish's exact placement — some describe Saint John Figtree as a small rural parish on Nevis, near Charlestown, others as sitting on Saint Kitts just northwest of Basseterre — but both point to a small, closely knit community where a visibly transgender visitor is unlikely to remain anonymous and gossip or outing exposure is a real concern. The surrounding social climate is conservatively Christian, and Nevis has a documented instance of official hostility at the point of entry: in 2005 port officials barred a cruise ship carrying mostly LGBTQ passengers and publicly framed the exclusion as a cultural decision. That incident is dated and does not establish current practice, and no recent trans-specific enforcement, arrests, violence, entry ban or facility restriction is documented for the parish. Tourism and reliance on outside visitors cut the other way, encouraging informal tolerance in hotels, restaurants and visitor-facing services. If identity becomes known, plausible consequences are misgendering, service friction or gossip, and in exceptional cases border questioning or refusal of admission; no severe punishment is documented, and there is no local protective machinery.

regions.name: Saint Mary Cayon

The parish is a small, rural coastal community on the central part of Saint Kitts, outside the main tourist belt around Basseterre and Frigate Bay, where limited resort infrastructure and close-knit surroundings make an outsider more visible than in urban or hotel areas. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes how a trans visitor would be treated here from the national picture, and nothing suggests a local protective exception or a local pattern of targeting either.

regions.name: Saint Paul Capisterre
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. Saint Paul Capisterre is a small, rural parish on Saint Kitts' northern coast, within reach of Basseterre and the island's main port and airport, made up of village-scale, church-going communities with very little tourist traffic. No local laws, border practices, facility rules or recorded incidents specific to the parish are known, so the practical picture rests on local social conditions rather than any change in the law. A visibly gender-nonconforming or trans visitor would likely stand out as an outsider in a tight-knit community where news travels fast, and anonymity and discretion are harder to maintain here than in Basseterre or the tourist belt. There are no known LGBTQ-specific venues, support services or advocacy groups locally, and day-to-day policing is thin. No pattern of anti-trans violence or state targeting of visitors has been recorded in the parish; document checks, visibility and social friction are the more plausible points of exposure, and the lack of recorded incidents should not be taken as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Saint Peter Basseterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint Peter Basseterre is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish covers the south-eastern side of Saint Kitts and holds the country's principal entry infrastructure: the capital Basseterre and its cruise port, the Robert L. Bradshaw International Airport, the eastern suburbs and the Frigate Bay resort belt, alongside smaller inland villages around St. Peter's. Document checks, immigration questioning and port discretion are concentrated here, so every visitor passes through this screening. Basseterre's tourism- and service-facing economy brings hotels, restaurants, cruise traffic and an expatriate presence; staff and other guests are used to foreigners, giving the town a more anonymous, cosmopolitan everyday feel than the federation's more conservative fringes, while the inland villages remain small, church-centred and socially conservative. Local descriptions of exposure focus on humiliation, service denial and administrative delay rather than physical violence. The documented 2005 exclusion of an LGBTQ cruise ship occurred at a Nevis port, not in this parish, and no local exclusion order, facility rule or ordinance specific to trans visitors is on record here; an outed visitor may still find no dependable local remedy.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Lowland
regions.merged_summary: Saint Thomas Lowland is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish sits on Nevis, a small, rural and largely churchgoing island of roughly twelve thousand people, where an openly trans visitor is highly visible and privacy is limited — community awareness of a trans guest is close to certain once outed. Nevis's upscale resort economy, serving international guests, offers comparatively neutral private settings, and the island's hospitality and tourism trade works in a visitor's favour. On that basis the foreseeable problems here are social and service-based rather than legal: refusals of lodging or service, misgendering, questioning during entry or port arrangements, and weak official follow-up, rather than any prosecution for identity or presentation. The country-level record on entry-point conduct remains the only documented official behaviour touching this island; no parish-specific border, facility, custody, care or violence practice is on record, how local officials would handle a mismatch on a foreign passport is uncertain, and no evidence of organised targeting or custodial risk has been recorded in this parish.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Middle Island
regions.merged_summary: Saint Thomas Middle Island is a small rural parish on the west coast of Saint Kitts, centred on Middle Island village and the Romney Manor/Caribelle Batik visitor sites, with a tight-knit, churchgoing population where a visibly transgender visitor stands out. The Saint Kitts and Nevis national regime applies here in full, with no local exception or separate parish-level rule. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this parish from the national picture: no parish-level enforcement practice, incident record, facility policy or protective measure is documented either way, and the absence of such records should not be read as safety. The documented refusal of an LGBTQ cruise ship occurred at a Nevis port, not in this parish.

regions.name: Trinity Palmetto Point
regions.merged_summary: Trinity Palmetto Point is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish sits on Saint Kitts's southeastern peninsula, a small, close-knit area with resort and yachting developments but little anonymous tourist infrastructure, so a trans visitor's presence is likely to be noticed by hosts, neighbours and service providers. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Trinity Palmetto Point from the national picture for Saint Kitts and Nevis, and no local trans-specific services, protections, or documented pattern of targeting are known here; visitors should expect everyday social or service friction rather than any locally distinct legal rule.

regions.name: Champasak
regions.merged_summary: Champasak is subject to Laos's national law in full, with no local exception. This southern province, centred on Pakse with the Mekong, the Wat Phou temple complex and the Si Phan Don islands, is tourist-facing, and guesthouses, hospitality staff and other foreign visitors are accustomed to outsiders, so an outed trans traveller is more likely to meet curiosity or awkwardness than organised hostility; guesthouse passport checks and provincial officialdom are the main everyday points of friction. Everyday difficulties are more likely to be misgendering, intrusive questioning and uneven hotel or clinic responses — hospitals and shared lodging may fall back on observed sex — rather than arrest, with no documented local pattern of police targeting or violence against trans visitors. Offsetting this, Champasak is small, rural and socially conservative, with stronger conservatism than the capital and less diplomatic visibility or support networks, and it has weak civil-society infrastructure with no trans-specific advocacy or visitor-facing complaint mechanism, so recourse if outed is thin: consequences are more likely to be social embarrassment, service disruption or discretionary public-order pressure than severe legal punishment. Distance from Vientiane and from NGO or diplomatic oversight compounds this, while national internet and media restrictions keep discussion of LGBTI issues quiet.

regions.name: Baalbek-Hermel
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exception. Baalbek-Hermel is a largely rural, socially conservative governorate in the Bekaa Valley, predominantly Shia, where tribal and honour norms and strong religious and party influence — particularly Hezbollah's, alongside Amal's — shape everyday conduct and operate as a de facto social and security authority. It lacks the LGBT venues, organisations, legal clinics, activist networks and anonymity available in Beirut: a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is conspicuous in a close-knit, clan-structured setting where discovery is likely to reach family or clan actors as well as police, and can escalate to detention, extortion or violence. Practical recourse is thinner than the national picture implies — lawyers, courts and consular help are harder to reach, police and local authorities are less protective and may be openly hostile, and no local protective measure, effective visitor-facing remedy or sympathetic judiciary is documented. Party and informal security actors have publicly opposed LGBT visibility, and a 2023 crackdown on LGBT cultural events indicates this hostility is active in the zone. No region-specific cases of trans enforcement in the governorate are documented, so local enforcement intensity is uncertain; that absence of recorded incidents should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Beyrouth
regions.merged_summary: Beyrouth is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exemption. Beirut is the country's most cosmopolitan and tourism-oriented city, concentrating its LGBTQ venues, NGOs such as Helem and Legal Agenda, and legal-aid support; its tourist and university districts offer more anonymity than rural areas, and social familiarity with gender diversity is greater than elsewhere in Lebanon. That visibility also concentrates policing and hostility: documented incidents in the city include raids on nightlife venues and gatherings, the 2018 security-forces shutdown of Beirut Pride, and extortion or mistreatment during identity checks, checkpoints and periods of public moral panic. Local tolerance is uneven and depends on district and authority, so consequences remain serious if an officer, landlord, venue staff or hostile group identifies a traveller as transgender. Identity documents that do not match presentation can draw added scrutiny, and travelling families with a child may face extra attention through guardianship, schools and neighbourhood reaction. Economic and institutional collapse has left official recourse thin, and court rulings have limited some prosecutions without guaranteeing equal treatment on the ground.

regions.name: Keserwan-Jbeil
regions.merged_summary: Keserwan-Jbeil is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate lies north of Beirut, taking in mountain interior and a tourist-facing coast around Jounieh, Harissa and Byblos, where hotels, beach resorts and a busy nightlife strip are accustomed to foreign visitors. It is predominantly Maronite Christian and generally more socially conservative than Beirut: strong church, family and village networks mean anonymity is harder to keep, so being outed can quickly become community or family pressure rather than a formal legal problem. There is no queer infrastructure, advocacy presence or organised venue scene of the Beirut kind, and legal aid and community networks are concentrated in the capital, leaving thinner recourse if something goes wrong. Security forces, courts and the civil registry operate here under the same national authority as elsewhere, and no local protective exception, sanctuary practice or distinct regional enforcement pattern has been documented — nor is there evidence of a local anti-LGBT campaign. Practical exposure runs through everyday checkpoints: document and identity checks, hotel registration, and social visibility in small communities. Tourist-area geography may soften day-to-day encounters with foreigners, but nothing local offsets the national framework, and local data on conditions for trans travellers is thin.

regions.name: Liban-Nord
regions.merged_summary: Liban-Nord operates fully under Lebanon's national legal framework on gender expression and public order, with no local exception or protective ordinance of its own. The north is markedly more religiously and socially conservative than Beirut: Tripoli and its smaller towns, the rural Akkar interior and other inland areas are close-knit and strongly sectarian, with Salafist influence reported in places and less tolerance of visible gender nonconformity. Support is thin - there is little visible LGBT community infrastructure, trans-specific advocacy or legal-aid presence of the kind found in the capital - and police protection for a visibly transgender visitor is described as less reliable, leaving fewer confidential channels for redress if someone is questioned, detained, harassed or assaulted. Discovery can spread quickly through family and community networks, so outing and informal pressure are more likely than in Beirut; confrontation, refusal of service, harassment or extortion are considered more probable, and a weaker rule-ofilfe environment plus a severe economic crisis compound this. Along the Batroun and coastal tourist belt, and in some coastal Christian towns, the atmosphere is more relaxed and used to foreign visitors, allowing somewhat more discretion - but no documented local tolerance measure or protective practice offsets these conditions anywhere in the region, and documentation demands remain a live outing risk.

regions.name: Mont-Liban
regions.merged_summary: Mont-Liban is subject to Lebanese national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate wraps around Beirut and takes in its inner and coastal suburbs, so much of the capital's nightlife spill-over, alongside tourist centres such as Byblos, Jounieh, Faraya and Aley. In these Beirut-adjacent urban and tourist-facing districts, trans and queer visibility is the highest in the country, nightlife and hospitality are comparatively tolerant, and activist and legal-aid organisations are close at hand — the strongest everyday privacy and support a traveller will find in Lebanon. Tourism-heavy areas are used to foreigners, which can make ordinary movement easier. Away from that corridor, the governorate mixes in strongly conservative Maronite, Druze and Shia communities where clerical and family authority is heavy and gender-nonconforming presentation draws open hostility; queer visibility and support services are far thinner there, and recourse is limited. Security forces operate under national Interior Ministry authority and no regional rule softens police powers, so street-level friction, hotel or landlord identity checks and refusal of service can still lead to interrogation, brief detention or a morality charge, with family or neighbours as likely a trigger as police initiative. Local enforcement appears uneven and may turn on discretion or community complaints, and documented rises in prejudice and violence as well as executive restrictions on public assembly have affected this metropolitan area directly. Net of the region's stronger community networks and discreet urban norms, exposure for a trans visitor remains driven by nationally enforced statutes rather than local tolerance.

regions.name: Gbarpolu
regions.merged_summary: Gbarpolu falls entirely under Liberia's national regime in full, with no local exception or additional local protection. This is a remote, forested and sparsely populated interior county centred on Bopolu, with a subsistence and small-scale mining economy, limited road access and little tourism. Police and court presence are thin and much day-to-day governance rests with customary authorities and community institutions, so anonymity is scarce: in small communities a visibly trans visitor who is discovered would likely meet intense local curiosity, social hostility, misrecognition, service refusal or community pressure rather than any institutional accommodation. Religious and customary conservatism is strong, health services are limited, and basic local custody arrangements would be likely to place a trans person according to birth sex. There is no trans or LGBTQ organisation or safe venue in the county, and the advocacy-run private spaces documented nationally are concentrated in Monrovia and not readily reachable from here. Help after harassment or extortion would be uncertain given the distance of police and services, and local incident reporting is sparse, so records of how national law is applied here are limited.

regions.name: Grand Bassa
regions.merged_summary: Grand Bassa is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a rural, tightly knit coastal area centred on the port city of Buchanan, more conservative and less institutionally supported than Monrovia, with the capital's advocacy organisations and private affirming spaces largely unavailable locally. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Grand Bassa's treatment of trans visitors, enforcement, or local protections from the national picture — an absence of evidence rather than a sign of safety.

regions.name: Grand Cape Mount
regions.merged_summary: Grand Cape Mount is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a sparsely populated western coastal area centred on Robertsport, where police posts, courts and health facilities are few and Monrovia's advocacy and support networks are a long journey away. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes conditions here from the national picture, so the country-level guidance applies unchanged; the absence of local reports should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Lofa
regions.merged_summary: Lofa lies within Liberia's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Lofa is a largely rural, comparatively remote county in Liberia's northwest, bordering Guinea and Sierra Leone, with Voinjama as its principal town and a scatter of small settlements and border communities; in such tightly networked places a visibly transgender visitor has little anonymity, and limited visitor traffic means encounters tend to be remembered rather than anonymous. Local conditions raise the consequences of discovery: communities are socially conservative, with Christian, Muslim and indigenous expectations alongside traditional authority structures, and there is little visible LGBTQ advocacy, anonymous private space or trans-specific support outside Monrovia, where the country's advocacy networks are concentrated. Policing and justice capacity in outlying areas is thin, so formal protection and practical recourse are limited — if police or courts become involved, weak local remedies offer little mitigation. Local risks reported for a visitor who is discovered include community exposure and outing within tight networks, stigma, and possible extortion. There is no documented pattern of Lofa-specific targeting or organised state hostility beyond the national picture, and no local protections, tolerance signals or safer venues distinguishing Lofa from the rest of the country have been identified.

regions.name: River Gee
regions.merged_summary: River Gee is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a remote, sparsely populated south-eastern district centred on Fish Town, with subsistence agriculture, limited tourism, thin police, medical and judicial capacity, and conservative Christian and traditional community norms — conditions that make privacy difficult for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor in small, closely-knit communities. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes River Gee from the national picture; matters such as local police practice, document checks, protective services or county-level safeguards are undocumented rather than established as safe. Practical consequences for a trans traveller follow the national climate: disclosure locally may meet social hostility with few nearby support networks or channels for remedy.

regions.name: Rivercess
regions.merged_summary: Rivercess County is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a sparsely populated rural county on the southeastern coast, with a logging and mining economy, little tourism infrastructure, and small, tight-knit communities where a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is noticed quickly and anonymity is hard to find. Customary chiefly authority carries much of daily governance, Christian churches dominate social life, and gender nonconformity is widely read as a moral failing rather than a private matter. Formal state presence is thin: police presence, judicial reach and medical infrastructure are all limited, with serious medical cases referred onward to Monrovia, so recourse after an outing is weaker here than in the capital and any detention would place a trans visitor by birth sex in a facility with no protective protocols. The country's LGBTQ-supportive spaces and advocacy networks, such as SAIL and TNOL, are concentrated in Monrovia and are not known to operate in Rivercess, leaving a visitor with no local community fallback; the employment nondiscrimination clause in the Decent Work Act has no realistic enforcement locally. No county-level protective exception, care access, or distinct pattern of identity-based enforcement is documented here — and the absence of local incident records should not be read as reassurance. Local conditions appear more conservative than in Monrovia and add exposure rather than protection, without any documented surge of added hostility.

regions.name: Anse la Raya
regions.merged_summary: Anse la Raye is a small west-coast quarter of fishing villages and modest local tourism. The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Anse la Raye from the national picture on policing, services, or social attitudes toward a transgender visitor.

regions.name: Canaries
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. Canaries is a small, tight-knit west-coast fishing village where a visibly trans visitor would have little anonymity and where policing, medical and legal services are centred in Castries or Soufrière. No local evidence was found that distinguishes Canaries from the national picture — no documented local ordinances, service-denial patterns or incidents specific to the area — and this lack of local documentation should not be read as either added safety or added danger.

regions.name: Dennery
regions.merged_summary: Dennery is subject to Saint Lucia's national legal regime in full, with no local exception or separate ordinance. It is a small, predominantly Creole-speaking fishing town on the Atlantic east coast, more rural, traditional and close-knit than Castries or the northwest resort belt, with modest tourism infrastructure, little visible LGBTQ presence and fewer trans-specific support or advocacy resources than the capital or the northern visitor areas. Local conditions shape how those national protections are experienced: a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner has far less anonymity here, so outing, staring, gossip, direct questioning, misgendering and service friction in everyday encounters are the more likely forms of exposure than state action. Social conservatism tied to religious attitudes persists in the community, and because complaint-handling and policing are less centralized and further from the trained units and services concentrated in Castries, familiarity with trans issues and consistency of enforcement are likely thinner and less predictable if a visitor needs to escalate a complaint. National police and court recourse remains available, and the tourism-dependent local economy generally accommodates foreign guests. No Dennery-specific incident, anti-trans campaign, local facility or document restriction has been documented, and no pattern of trans-specific violence or detention is known here — but that absence of local evidence should not be read as a guarantee of safety.

regions.name: Laborie
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. Laborie is a small, quiet fishing and farming community on the island's southwestern coast, close to Hewanorra airport and Vieux Fort and well away from the resort corridors and LGBT infrastructure of Castries and Gros Islet. It is a tight-knit traditional Creole and Catholic village where anonymity is hard to keep: everyone is known, gossip travels fast, and a visibly transgender visitor should expect curiosity, informal questioning, misgendering and possible awkwardness in local services rather than organised or state hostility. Local medical and transport infrastructure is limited, and trained officers and institutional support are concentrated in the capital, so an incident would draw community attention before institutional help. Violent crime is low and no case of trans-targeted policing, service refusal or violence in Laborie has been documented — but that reflects an unrecorded local record rather than demonstrated safety, and discretion about visibility remains sensible.

regions.name: Micoud

No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Micoud from the national picture — there is no documented local record of police conduct, facility practice, or incidents involving transgender visitors. Where documentation is silent, that silence should not be read as evidence of safety, and any local social conditions a visitor encounters remain unrecorded here.

regions.name: Vieux Fort
regions.merged_summary:
Vieux Fort is a small, close-knit southern coastal town and Saint Lucia's principal international gateway, home to Hewanorra International Airport, so routine immigration and document checks are the first national procedures most visitors meet; no local practice of targeting transgender travellers or rejecting foreign documents is known. The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions matter more than any legal difference here. The town's beach resorts, dive operators and visitor nightlife create a tourism-facing setting where hospitality workers used to international guests tend to prioritise service, which can soften everyday friction for a gender-nonconforming traveller. At the same time Vieux Fort is smaller and more socially conservative than Castries or Gros Islet, shaped by church and community norms and offering limited anonymity: a visibly trans visitor may face stares, gossip, misgendering, service friction or verbal hostility in streets, clubs and informal settings, with outcomes depending heavily on individual attitudes and discretion. There is no local trans-specific protocol, advocacy infrastructure or documented local protection — support services are concentrated in Castries. No documented pattern of anti-trans violence or official hostility toward visitors exists locally, and the anti-LGBT violence on the national record has been orientation-motivated. Police and border conduct follow national rather than locally tailored practice, while areas such as facility access and custody placement are simply undocumented; that uncertainty is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Balzers
regions.merged_summary: Balzers is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. It is Liechtenstein's southernmost municipality, a small, predominantly Catholic rural community of a few thousand residents near the Swiss border, known for Gutenberg Castle and vineyards, with a quiet, tourism-facing character and close practical ties to Switzerland. Its small size and tight-knit society mean a visibly trans visitor is more noticeable here than in larger towns: local sources suggest everyday friction — staring, misgendering, awkward hotel or clinic interactions, and conservative disapproval — is somewhat likelier than in Vaduz or Schaan, and the modest scale of local institutions can limit discreet recourse. There is no documented Balzers-specific policing, exclusion rule, hostility, or violence directed at trans people; police and courts are functional, with a strong rule-of-law tradition, and no local ordinance restricting facilities or targeting gender-nonconforming visitors exists. Beyond national protections, no additional local safeguard is recorded either, so the practical exposure here is social discomfort and institutional uncertainty rather than state or organised threat, with casual curiosity common in a community of this size.

regions.name: Eschen

No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Eschen from the national picture on policing, facilities access, discrimination or official attitudes.

regions.name: Gamprin

Gamprin is a small, low-lying rural commune on the Rhine in the Oberland, close-knit and without its own police force or services aimed at trans visitors, where a visibly trans traveller may meet curiosity or awkwardness rather than organised hostility. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Gamprin from the national picture: policing, border control and document practice are national, and no local ordinance, documented incident or pattern of targeting specific to this municipality is known.

regions.name: Mauren
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. Mauren is a small, predominantly rural and residential municipality with a close-knit, strongly Roman Catholic social character, and it has no separate municipal law or police force. No region-specific evidence was found to distinguish Mauren from the national picture. Local conditions add visibility rather than a distinct legal exposure: a visibly trans visitor may draw curiosity, bureaucratic inexperience or service friction in a small community where anonymity is limited, though no documented local pattern of refusals, police targeting or trans-specific violence is known — and such silence is not itself evidence of safety. No trans-specific local support organisation is known.

regions.name: Ruggell
regions.merged_summary: Ruggell falls under Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. Ruggell is Liechtenstein's smallest and northernmost municipality, a quiet, predominantly Catholic Rhine-valley village near the Swiss border; its close-knit, low-anonymity setting may mean greater social visibility and scrutiny than a larger town would bring, though no documented local police targeting, organised hostility, or violence against trans visitors is known.

regions.name: Schaan
regions.merged_summary:
Schaan, Liechtenstein's largest municipality and its commercial and transport centre adjoining Vaduz near the Swiss border, is subject to Liechtenstein national law in full, with no local exception.

Locally it is an affluent, low-crime Alpine town with a tourism- and business-oriented, internationally connected economy; daily interaction is generally tolerant, and police and courts operate predictably. No municipality-level rule on facilities, documents or public conduct targeting gender identity is known, and no documented pattern of police targeting, violent targeting or organised harassment of trans visitors has been recorded there. Its size, anonymity and visitor-facing character may reduce overt harassment compared with smaller rural communes. Against that, the state's Catholic-conservative climate — reflected in official and religious discourse — colours the setting, so a trans visitor's practical exposure is more likely to be social friction, service-level discretion and bureaucratic mismatch than state action, and such friction is difficult to resolve locally. Incident data specific to trans visitors in Schaan are scarce, so this account reflects observed local conditions rather than a documented record of incidents.

regions.name: Schellenberg
regions.merged_summary: Schellenberg is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. The municipality is a small, rural community of roughly a thousand residents in the Rhine lowlands — traditionally Catholic and agrarian, where an unfamiliar face readily draws notice in a compact village setting. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes conditions for trans visitors here from the national picture: no local statute, policing practice, facility rule or documented incident specific to the municipality is on record. That lack of local detail should not be read as reassurance — it means the country-level regime and the social climate described there are what a visitor will actually encounter.

regions.name: Triesen
regions.merged_summary: Triesen falls squarely under Liechtenstein's national regime, with no local legal variation of its own. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes the municipality from the country-level picture: there are no local ordinances, protective measures, documented enforcement practices, or recorded incidents involving transgender visitors. The municipality is a small residential town in the Rhine valley near Vaduz, with a predominantly Catholic, socially conservative character in which being visibly gender-nonconforming may attract ordinary small-town curiosity, though no local hostility or state targeting is documented.

regions.name: Triesenberg
regions.merged_summary: Triesenberg is a small alpine municipality in Liechtenstein's Oberland, rising above Vaduz and taking in the Malbun resort area, where tourism is a mainstay of a compact, rural and predominantly Roman Catholic community. The region is subject to Liechtenstein national law in full, with no local exception. No Triesenberg-specific ordinances, police practices or patterns of targeting against trans visitors are documented, and national policing and courts operate predictably, so escalation into detention, prosecution, violence or denial of care appears unlikely. The main local difference is social rather than legal: in a close-knit village setting, disclosure or being recognised is more noticeable than in the capital, and a trans visitor may encounter staring, curiosity, misgendering, informal judgment or service awkwardness rather than open hostility. The surrounding conservative social climate and Catholic character of the municipality mean such friction is plausible, though local attitudes and trans visitors' actual experiences in Triesenberg remain thinly documented; absence of reported incidents should not be read as evidence of welcome.

regions.name: Vaduz
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. Vaduz is the country's capital and largest town, the seat of government, courts and financial-sector employers, and its main tourism-facing centre, with a substantial cross-border and expatriate workforce, close Swiss influence and functioning public institutions; the anonymity of a small urban centre and the flow of international visitors make ordinary interactions easier than in outlying villages. What a visibly trans visitor is likelier to notice is social rather than official: Vaduz sits within a small, Catholic and socially conservative society where staring, curiosity or disapproval can occur, and social friction is more likely than confrontation. No documented pattern of police targeting, extortion, custody abuse or anti-trans violence against visitors is recorded in the capital, and no local policy diverging from the national picture is known. Discovery through document mismatch at Schengen entry or hotel registration remains possible, and the national position on legal remedies applies here unchanged.

regions.name: Central Province
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sri Lanka's national law in full, with no local exception. Central Province covers Kandy, Matale and the hill country around Nuwara Eliya; it is the island's religious and cultural heartland, centred on the Temple of the Tooth, and its Sinhalese and Tamil hill communities — including Nuwara Eliya's plantation areas — hold strong temple-influenced moral conservatism that runs deeper than in Colombo, so trans visibility is likely to draw social scrutiny and moral policing. Policing is thinner and more traditional than in the Western Province, and there are fewer community organisations, NGOs or predictable complaint-handling routes than in the capital, leaving a traveller who is outed with less recourse. Kandy's established tourism economy and hotel sector give some foreigner-tolerance and service-sector familiarity, but they offer no legal protection, and no province-specific protection or dedicated trans support is documented anywhere in the province. Kandy also holds Bogambara Prison, where anyone arrested would be accommodated under national arrangements. No region-specific record of trans-targeted enforcement, facility rules or violence distinct from the national picture has been documented locally; that uncertainty should not be read as safety. The main local exposure is police-driven discovery, service friction and possible short custody rather than imprisonment for identity alone.

regions.name: Eastern Province
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sri Lanka's national law in full, with no local exception. Eastern Province — Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Ampara — is largely rural and poorer than Colombo, with a predominantly Tamil and Muslim population and stronger social and religious conservatism than the capital, where LGBTQ advocacy, legal aid and community organisations are concentrated. Tighter-knit communities mean a visibly gender-nonconforming or foreign trans visitor attracts curiosity and scrutiny, and anonymity after being outed is limited. A heavy post-war security presence, including frequent police and military checkpoints, raises everyday document-check exposure, and police in the province carry a strong security mandate with a poor accountability culture; moral policing is reported as sharper in Muslim-majority areas such as Kalmunai and Ampara. Trans-focused health, advocacy and legal-aid infrastructure is thin, so an outed traveller has fewer local allies and weaker practical recourse than in the capital. Tourist areas differ in everyday texture: Trincomalee's tourism and naval activity, and enclaves such as Arugam Bay, are more used to foreigners and may offer some anonymity and greater leniency in casual encounters. That everyday tolerance does not extend to encounters with police, medics, prison officials or service providers, where discovery can lead to questioning, harassment, extortion or detention. No province-specific protection, remedy or documented pattern of trans-targeted violence is known to operate here, and the absence of such evidence reflects limited local documentation rather than a demonstrated safeguard.

regions.name: North Central Province
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sri Lanka's national law in full, with no local exception, and no province-specific protective measure or documented local enforcement pattern has been identified. North Central Province is the island's most rural and among its poorest areas, a dry-zone heartland built around the sacred Buddhist cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa. Heritage and pilgrimage tourism brings foreign visitors to these sites, but the province has none of Colombo's visible queer community organisations, outreach services, legal aid or tolerant commercial venues; support services are concentrated in provincial centres. Social attitudes are markedly more conservative than in the capital, with the Buddhist clergy a strong public presence and pronounced modesty expectations at religious sites. Everyday anonymity is thinner than in coastal or urban tourism, so a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming visitor may attract sustained local attention, and an outing would leave little informal recourse or community backup. The national police operate here as elsewhere with no local mitigation, so custody, extortion or assault risks in an encounter with authorities follow the national pattern, though imprisonment or lethal harm is not the typical outcome. No organised regional campaign against LGBT people is known.

regions.name: North Western Province
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sri Lanka's national law in full, with no local exception. North Western Province covers the Kurunegala and Puttalam districts and is largely rural and socially conservative, with thinner advocacy, medical and legal-aid infrastructure than Colombo; a small tourism pocket around Kalpitiya is the main visitor-facing exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this province from the national picture, and that absence of evidence should not be read as safer conditions — the national regime remains the relevant basis for a visit here, and no local protective measure or documented province-level hostility offsets it.

regions.name: Western Province
regions.merged_summary: Western Province — Colombo, Gampaha and Kalutara — falls under Sri Lanka's national regime in full, with no documented local exception and no province-specific screening of trans visitors recorded. It is the country's most urbanised and tourist-facing area: Colombo's international hotels, nightlife and dense street life give foreign visitors a degree of anonymity, gender-diverse presentation is comparatively familiar there, and hospitality-sector norms alongside a visible trans and gender-diverse community soften casual service discrimination relative to rural districts. Street-level curiosity toward a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is more likely to be friction than confrontation. The province also holds the country's largest concentration of LGBTQ community organisations and advocacy services, and much of the NGO and police-sensitisation activity, so complaints and support have slightly more institutional contact points than elsewhere. Against this, Colombo hosts major police and remand facilities where national custody practices apply directly, and police use of the criminal provisions as a lever against gender-nonconforming people has been documented within Colombo itself. Practical exposure points for a visibly trans visitor include hotel identity checks, nightlife policing and document stops: everyday comfort is modestly above the national picture, but recourse remains weak once authorities are involved.

regions.name: Berea District
regions.merged_summary: Berea District is subject to Lesotho's national law in full, with no local exception. The district adjoins Maseru, with Teyateyaneng as its seat, and mixes small-town, peri-urban and mountain-rural terrain with regular visitor traffic. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Berea District from the national picture: no district-level law, documented incident or official posture specific to the area appears in the record, and policing is the national Lesotho Mounted Police Service, so the country-level information applies here without local modification.

regions.name: Butha-Buthe District
regions.merged_summary: Butha-Buthe District is subject to Lesotho's national law in full, with no local exception. The district covers Lesotho's rural, mountainous north, taking in a small district capital and a South African border post where documents are checked. It is a traditional, church-influenced highland area of small communities where anonymity is scarce: gossip travels quickly, and a transgender visitor who is recognised can become a matter of community-wide attention rather than a private one. Police, clinics, lodgings and community leaders here have less familiarity with transgender visitors than their counterparts in the capital, and no local LGBTI organisation is known — support structures concentrate in Maseru, so recourse after a refusal of service, misgendering, hostile curiosity or insensitive policing is thinner and slower to arrive. There is no district-specific protective exception, and no documented record of organised anti-trans targeting, custodial campaigns or lethal violence in the district; that absence reflects limited documentation rather than confirmed safety. The Matrix Support Group's cooperative relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service is recorded nationally and covers work in all ten districts, offering some route to recourse, though the documented instances of police support come from Maseru. The practical exposure here is social and administrative rather than criminal, magnified by remoteness.

regions.name: Mafeteng District
regions.merged_summary:
Mafeteng District sits in Lesotho's southern lowlands: a small, largely rural district organised around an agricultural town rather than the capital. The region is subject to Lesotho's national regime in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions shape how that regime is experienced. Communities here are close-knit and traditionally conservative, so a visibly gender-nonconforming or openly trans visitor is likely to draw attention, gossip and possible social or familial confrontation, with far less anonymity than in Maseru. The district has little of the capital's visible LGBT-friendly infrastructure, and support services, legal help and accommodation choices are concentrated in Maseru, leaving a visitor dependent on close family and community networks and on local institutions whose responsiveness can be uneven. The national LGBTI support organisation's presence reaches all districts including Mafeteng and has a cooperative history with the national police service, but its contact with everyday district-level policing is thin. No documented local ordinance, raid or targeted enforcement against trans visitors is known from Mafeteng; that absence of records should not be read as evidence of safety, since community-level hostility and underreporting remain the more realistic local exposure than formal legal jeopardy.

regions.name: Mohale's Hoek District
regions.merged_summary: Mohale's Hoek District is subject to Lesotho's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this district from the national picture, so the country-level guidance above applies here as written — and the absence of district-level records should not be read as reassurance. The district is a small, rural southern area a distance from Maseru, where anonymity is limited and the capital's LGBTI organisations, visible queer infrastructure and supportive police encounters are less readily reached.

regions.name: Klaipeda County
regions.merged_summary: Klaipeda County is subject to Lithuania's national law in full, with no local exception. Locally, the county takes in the port city of Klaipeda — Lithuania's third-largest city and a major seaport — along with the coastal resorts of Palanga and the Curonian Spit, a tourism- and service-oriented area receiving many foreign visitors. That urban, coastal and tourist-facing character means visitor-facing services have some familiarity with travellers and anonymity is higher than in rural Lithuania, so everyday friction tends to be somewhat lighter than in the countryside. Local conditions otherwise differ only modestly from the national picture: no local ordinance, enforcement pattern or trans-specific incident record distinguishing the county is documented. The city is smaller and socially more provincial than Vilnius, with weaker trans-specific support and complaint practice, and schools or clinics may be slower to accommodate a trans visitor, particularly where a minor is involved. Where a visitor's identity becomes known, the likely exposures are awkward questioning, service friction, misgendering and social disapproval against a socially conservative backdrop, with limited local recourse, rather than any distinct legal or custodial threat specific to the county.

regions.name: Canton Capellen
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Luxembourg's national regime in full, with no local exception. Canton Capellen is an affluent, largely residential and commuter belt west of Luxembourg City, taking in small towns and villages such as Mamer, Capellen, Kehlen, Käerjeng and Steinfort, with a substantial international and cross-border population — particularly around Mamer, Capellen and Kehlen — and high everyday exposure to foreign residents. No cantonal or communal ordinances restricting gender expression, facilities or services are known, no local policing or tourist-facing practice differs from the national picture, and no trans-specific incidents have been documented there. Practical friction would come from ordinary rural-urban variation in familiarity: in smaller villages, social conservatism may occasionally produce curiosity or misgendering rather than hostility. Luxembourg's compact, well-policed environment means national institutions operate throughout the canton, with the equality body and the national LGBTIQ+ centre based a short distance away in Luxembourg City. One local practical gap: the canton has no acute hospital, so more specialised care requires travel toward the capital.

regions.name: Canton Clervaux
regions.merged_summary: Canton Clervaux falls entirely under Luxembourg's national legal framework, with no local ordinance, facility rule or enforcement practice known to depart from it. Clervaux is a small, sparsely populated rural canton in the northern Ösling, centred on Clervaux town and its castle and Christmas market, with tourism as a mainstay of local life. Its social climate is Catholic-influenced and comparatively traditional, and in a tight-knit community there is far less anonymity than in Luxembourg City: a trans visitor may attract staring, curiosity, misgendering or awkward conversations at small hotels, parish events, markets or with community groups, and being noticed carries more social exposure than in the capital — including for a family or travelling minor, where discovery is a social rather than a legal problem. No trans-specific targeting, police hostility, facility exclusion or organised hostility toward visitors is documented in the canton, but neither is there region-specific evidence about how trans visitors are actually treated in local accommodations, services or border encounters, and that silence should not be read as assurance. Functional courts and national equality complaint routes remain available if friction escalates.

regions.name: Canton Diekirch
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Luxembourg's national law in full, with no local exception. Canton Diekirch is the country's northern rural canton, covering the Éislek and Oesling around the town of Diekirch and the smaller municipalities of Vianden, an older and more traditionally Catholic population with an agricultural, small-town character rather than the anonymity of Luxembourg City. LGBTIQ+ support organisations and visibly queer infrastructure concentrate in the capital, so a trans visitor here has fewer local support points, though care is available through the regional hospital and national complaints and police channels remain operative. Everyday familiarity with trans identities is lower than in the city, and lesser anonymity means a visibly trans visitor may attract ordinary curiosity, awkward bureaucratic handling, misgendering or conservative social friction; no local ordinance, policing practice, exclusion rule or documented pattern of targeting trans visitors is known to depart from the national framework, and no canton-specific restrictions have been identified. The practical difference is one of service depth and social reserve rather than any change in legal standing or recourse.

regions.name: Canton Echternach
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Luxembourg's national law in full, with no local exception. Canton Echternach is a small, rural eastern canton in the Mullerthal region, centred on the town of Echternach with its lake and abbey, and its tourist-oriented economy brings routine contact with foreign visitors. No cantonal or communal ordinance restricts facilities, documents or service access here, and no local pattern of anti-trans enforcement, hostility or visitor-directed violence is documented. Police and communal services are the same national institutions operating elsewhere in the country. Practical differences are social rather than legal: in a tight-knit, historically Catholic, tourism-oriented population of roughly nineteen thousand, an outed visitor is more conspicuous, and everyday visibility of trans people, specialised community services and institutional familiarity with gender-identity paperwork are lower than in Luxembourg City. The main local risks, conditional on discovery, are discomfort, curiosity, awkward misgendering or bureaucratic unfamiliarity rather than legal punishment — social friction in a small community, not hostility. National rule-of-law remedies and the equality body remain operative for a traveller here. The absence of documented local problems should not be read as proof that none can occur, and the available information does not establish how consistently protections play out in every local encounter.

regions.name: Canton Grevenmacher
regions.merged_summary: Canton Grevenmacher is subject to Luxembourg's national regime in full, with no local exception: it has no separate cantonal rules on recognition, documents, policing, facilities or care. The canton covers eastern Luxembourg along the Moselle and Sûre valleys on the German border, taking in Grevenmacher, Remich, Wormeldange and Echternach — a quiet, largely rural, traditionally Catholic wine-growing area of small towns with a tourism economy, steady foreign visitors and cross-border commuters. Outside the capital, anonymity is lower, so staring, everyday curiosity or an awkward service encounter in a wine village is more plausible than in Luxembourg City; social visibility of a diverse traveller is moderate rather than cosmopolitan. There is no documented pattern of police hostility, targeted enforcement, facility exclusion, service refusal or violence toward gender-nonconforming people, and national institutions and courts operate normally here as elsewhere. That said, local incident and attitude data is thin, so the absence of reported problems should not be read as proof of safety, and how consistently national protections operate in practice on the ground is not established by local evidence.

regions.name: Canton Mersch
regions.merged_summary: Canton Mersch is subject to Luxembourg's national law in full, with no local exception. A quiet, semi-rural central canton of small towns and commuter villages on the main rail line to Luxembourg City, it has no separate civil-registry, policing, healthcare or border rules of its own: no local ordinance restricts gender expression, no documented pattern of police or official hostility toward trans visitors exists, and complaints, courts and equality recourse run through the national institutions, which function normally here. On the everyday level, the canton's smaller communities offer less anonymity than the capital — fewer visible community venues, less nearby trans-specific support, and a mildly more conservative, small-town social climate where an outed visitor might reasonably expect staring, curiosity, awkwardness or hesitant service reactions. There is, however, no evidence of local targeting, exclusion from facilities, or escalation to serious harm, and the canton sits on well-trafficked routes with quick access to Luxembourg City's community services and support organisations.

regions.name: Canton Remich
regions.merged_summary: Canton Remich is subject to Luxembourg's national law in full, with no local exception. Local conditions, rather than local rules, are what distinguish the canton: Remich is a small, affluent, low-crime Moselle wine district on the French and German borders, built around vineyards, quiet riverside towns and a cross-border tourism economy that depends on welcoming visitors from both sides. It is more rural and less cosmopolitan than Luxembourg City, with less everyday anonymity — a visibly trans visitor in a small village or a family-run hospitality business may be recognised, stared at or met with bemusement, awkwardness, conservative attitudes or limited staff familiarity. Assessments describe this as social friction rather than hostility, and record no local pattern of service refusal, police hostility or state-imposed exclusion. Specialised trans health care and LGBT support are thinner than in the capital, and everyday services in the canton operate on the same basis as elsewhere, with national complaint and support channels reachable regardless of locality. No canton-specific ordinance, facility restriction, screening practice or documented police targeting of trans visitors was identified here, though the small scale of local research means local enforcement practice is not confirmed in detail.

regions.name: Canton Vianden
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Luxembourg's national framework in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Canton Vianden's treatment of transgender visitors from the national picture: no canton-specific border practice, facility rule, enforcement pattern or documented incident is on record. The canton is a small, rural, tourism-oriented area in the north-east near the German border, centred on a historic town and castle; a visitor there is simply more visible and anonymity thinner than in Luxembourg City, and any friction would more plausibly stem from small-community unfamiliarity than from any known local hostility, with recourse running through the country's national equality and support services.

regions.name: Alūksnes novads
regions.merged_summary: Alūksnes novads is subject to Latvia's national regime in full, with no local exception of its own. It is a small, sparsely populated and still-shrinking rural municipality in the northeast, centred on the lakeside town of Alūksne near the Estonian and Russian borders, where a lakeside tourism trade brings some visitors but everyday life is quiet and familiar. Municipal authorities here hold no power over entry documents, facility rules or criminal law, and no local ordinance, policing practice or documented incident involving a trans visitor is known. No local LGBT community infrastructure, trans-specific support or specialist legal aid exists; practical help, English-speaking staff and complaint channels are thinner than in Riga, and recourse for anything serious effectively runs through capital institutions. Socially the area is more conservative than the capital, with limited public visibility of trans life, so anonymity is low: an outed visitor is more likely to meet staring, intrusive questions, misgendering, service friction and unsympathetic local handling than state targeting. The realistic exposure is therefore discrimination, inconvenience and low-level hostility rather than arrest or organised persecution, and small-town reporting of bias-motivated complaints may be slow or hard to pursue.

regions.name: Augšdaugavas novads
regions.merged_summary:
Augšdaugavas novads is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception.

The municipality is a largely rural, Russian-speaking part of Latgale in southeastern Latvia, wrapping around the city of Daugavpils and running to the Belarus border; Daugavpils itself is administratively separate from the novads, and the Daugavpils attack investigation referenced in Latvia's national profile concerned the city rather than this municipality. Border-area identity checks are common enough that a mismatch between documents and presentation can surface during ordinary travel. Socially the area is more conservative than Riga, with small close-knit communities, fewer anonymity options, little tourism, and very thin specialised trans or LGBT service provision, so an outed visitor is likely to depend on the discretion of individual police officers or clinic staff and to face slower recourse than in the capital. In practice this can mean staring, intrusive questions or refused service in everyday encounters, and weaker first-instance police help, though national prosecutors and courts remain available if a complaint is mishandled. No local anti-trans ordinance, facility ban, or organised local targeting is known, and no incident record specific to the novads has been identified — a gap in documentation rather than evidence that local conditions are more forgiving. Hostility reported in the wider area has not been shown to follow a trans-specific pattern, and conditions do not indicate systematic state persecution.

regions.name: Daugavpils
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception. Daugavpils is Latvia's second-largest city, in the eastern Latgale region, with a large Russian-speaking population; assessments describe it as more socially conservative and less cosmopolitan than Riga, with a more reserved social climate for an openly trans visitor, no record of Pride or other visible LGBT infrastructure, and fewer of the support networks found in the capital. The Rothko Art Centre and ordinary hospitality draw visitors, and practical exposure here centres on how people and police react rather than on any legal penalty. The clearest local concern is the handling of prejudice-driven violence: in an attack on two people in the city, police closed the investigation and the Prosecutor General had to order it reopened — suggesting local recourse can be delayed or uneven. No Daugavpils-specific restriction on gender expression, facilities, border handling or custody practice, and no organised targeting or surveillance of trans visitors, is documented; that thinness of local evidence is not reassurance in itself, and the practical risk for a visitor who is outed remains social friction and uncertain police response.

regions.name: Ludzas novads
regions.merged_summary: Ludzas novads is subject to Latvia's national legal regime in full, with no local exception or local provision of its own. It is a small, sparsely populated, predominantly Russian-speaking rural municipality in eastern Latvia's Latgale region, on the Russian and Belarusian border, with little tourism, less urban anonymity than Riga or Daugavpils, and far fewer specialist health services, support organisations and LGBTQ infrastructure. For a trans visitor that combination means disclosure is more likely: in smaller communities a visibly gender-nonconforming or foreign visitor can expect staring, intrusive curiosity and low-level hostility rather than the anonymity of the capital. Border proximity adds document checks at crossings. Practically, recourse is thinner — specialist care, legal aid and advocacy organisations are a long way off, so outcomes lean heavily on the attitudes of individual officers and staff, and harassment is more likely to go quietly unaddressed than in Riga. No trans-specific incident, hostile local legislation or documented targeting by local police is found for Ludzas novads; that reflects thin local reporting and the absence of a documented record rather than established safety, and conservative social norms around the visitor's everyday exposure should not be read as reassurance.

regions.name: Līvānu novads
regions.merged_summary: Līvānu novads is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a small, rural municipality in Latgale in eastern Latvia, home to roughly 11,000 people, with a limited service sector and a small-town character; no local ordinance, facility rule, checkpoint practice, or documented incident specific to transgender visitors has been identified, and police and officials are recorded applying national law without local targeting. The practical differences from Riga are social rather than legal: communities here are likely more conservative and less accustomed to transgender travellers, anonymity is limited in a close-knit area, and there is no trans-specific support infrastructure or known LGBTQ venue, so a visibly trans visitor may draw curiosity and find discreet accommodation or services hard to locate. Likely local exposures are social discomfort, misgendering, awkward treatment in shops or accommodation, and the possibility of a slow or unsympathetic official response if harassment occurs; organised hostility is not documented. Rural distance from larger centres weakens informal support and leaves thinner practical recourse, without adding state punishment beyond the national framework.

regions.name: Mārupes novads
regions.merged_summary: Mārupes novads is a largely residential, comparatively affluent suburban municipality immediately west of and adjoining Riga, and it contains Riga International Airport, so most visitors meet the area through the country's main international gateway. The region is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception.\n\nNo municipal ordinance, local policing practice or documented incident specific to the municipality sets it apart from the national picture, and there is no record of local targeting of gender-nonconforming people. What is distinctive here is the setting rather than the rules: a low-profile, family-oriented suburb with limited local trans organizing compared with the capital, where a visibly trans visitor may draw more staring, discomfort or bureaucratic confusion than in Riga itself, and where any response still runs through national institutions. Practical friction is most likely to surface at the airport and in hotels, where documents that do not match expectations can prompt extra questions. Proximity to Riga slightly eases access to police, courts and health services if something goes wrong, while the surrounding social climate is more conventional than in the capital. The area is urbanised, Riga-integrated and transit-facing, with no documented harsher local enforcement.

regions.name: Olaines novads
regions.merged_summary: Olaines novads is subject to Latvia's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. The municipality is a small industrial suburb just south of Riga, with a partly Russophone, working-class population and commuter links to the capital, where a visibly trans visitor may attract curiosity in a small-town setting while Riga's services remain a short trip away. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this municipality from the national picture, and the absence of local reports should not be read as evidence that discrimination or service friction is absent.

regions.name: Preiļu novads
regions.merged_summary:
Preiļu novads is subject to Latvia's national regime in full, with no local exception.

The municipality is a small, low-density rural district in Latgale, eastern Latvia, centred on Preiļi, with predominantly Latvian- and Russian-speaking, largely Catholic communities, modest tourism, limited nightlife and few specialist services compared with Riga. A visibly transgender visitor would stand out: in a small, low-anonymity community, attention, gossip, misgendering or friction over documents or services is more likely than in the capital, and local officials and police are unlikely to have specific trans-awareness training. There is no known local trans community or advocacy infrastructure to turn to, and police and legal responses outside towns tend to be slower, making practical remedies for harassment or refusal of service harder to reach even where national courts remain theoretically available.

No local ordinance adds restrictions, and no local pattern of trans-specific targeting, hostile legislation or violence is documented in Preiļu novads; the nearby city of Daugavpils does have a documented case in which police closed a homophobic attack investigation before the Prosecutor General ordered it reopened. The realistic exposure here is therefore social and administrative — visibility, gossip, possible harassment or refusal of service — rather than state persecution, but the absence of local incidents should not be read as reassurance, since limited documentation and thin local infrastructure also mean such problems are unlikely to be recorded or addressed.

regions.name: Ropažu novads
regions.merged_summary: Ropažu novads is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a quiet, semi-rural and commuter municipality adjoining Riga, with settlements such as Ropaži, Stopiņi, Vangaži and Garkalne. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this municipality from the national picture: no local ordinances, incidents, hostile enforcement patterns or protective provisions specific to transgender visitors are documented, and local policing, health and visitor-service practices are simply undocumented rather than known to be safe. Whatever applies at country level therefore applies here as it stands.

regions.name: Rēzeknes
regions.merged_summary:
Rēzekne is a small, economically depressed regional centre in Latgale, eastern Latvia, with a predominantly Russian-speaking population and strong Orthodox and Old Believer influence; the region is less urban, more religiously conservative and less tourist-facing than Riga or Jūrmala, with limited visible LGBTQ support infrastructure. The country-level regime applies here in full, with no local exception. No local rule imposes special restrictions on trans visitors, and nothing documented distinguishes Rēzeknes on border checks, facilities or document practice; the Daugavpils case noted at country level arose in this same region.

What differs locally is social exposure and the response to it. In a small community with little trans visibility, a visitor read as trans is likely to draw staring, intrusive questions, misgendering, possible refusal of service and low-level harassment rather than formal action. Police and prosecutors are less accustomed to gender-identity complaints, and thin civil-society capacity means an outed visitor has weak practical recourse; social conservatism and limited enforcement capacity leave local protection below the national average. There is no evidence of organised targeting, police campaigns or local criminalisation directed at trans visitors in Rēzeknes.

regions.name: Rēzeknes novads
regions.merged_summary: Rēzeknes novads is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception. The municipality covers rural eastern Latvia in the Latgale region, close to the Russian border: it is small, predominantly Russian-speaking and more religiously conservative, with strong Catholic and Orthodox observance, than Riga. Communities are close-knit with little anonymous urban space, so an outed visitor is likelier to meet staring, awkward misgendering, service hesitation or verbal harassment, and word travels quickly in small towns. The district has no LGBT-facing venues, no trans-aware clinics or specialist support services, and thinner local policing, legal aid and oversight than the capital; document checks at hotels, border posts or routine stops remain the most realistic outing vector, and recourse through local authorities may be slow or uneven. No municipal ordinance targeting gender expression or trans visitors is known, and no trans-specific incident or local enforcement action has been identified here — but that absence of documentation reflects limited local reporting rather than demonstrated protection. Border practices, facility access and local remedies for trans visitors are not documented for this municipality.

regions.name: Valkas novads
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Latvia's national law in full, with no local exception.
