The province wraps around the capital and takes in the port city of Nampo, the industrial and military centre of Pyongsong, and the overland approaches to Pyongyang; it is heavily industrialised and effectively closed to independent tourism, with no foreign-facing infrastructure beyond tightly chaperoned, state-arranged visits. Residents and visitors live under dense internal security, and the province carries a heavier internal-security character than Pyongyang's monitored showcase zone, so a trans visitor would be conspicuous and continuously accompanied. Nothing here offers a tolerant enclave or any documented local protection, and discovery would route directly into the national security apparatus rather than into any local remedy. Practically, a mismatch in documents or presentation is likely to surface during checks, guide reporting or interrogation, with possible confiscation of papers and devices, involvement of police or security officials, expulsion or arbitrary confinement, and no independent support available locally. Proximity to the capital intensifies surveillance and ideological conformity enforcement rather than easing it: the province's low visibility and lack of tourist or advocacy infrastructure give no protection once identity surfaces.

regions.name: AVEIRO
regions.merged_summary: Aveiro is subject to Portugal's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Aveiro is a compact coastal district built around a university city and a year-round visitor economy spanning the lagoon bars, Costa Nova and nearby beach resorts, giving travellers contact with a young, internationally exposed population and a tourism-facing service culture. The district sits in the more socially conservative and traditionally Catholic north, where Chega has polled strongly, and smaller-city scale can raise visibility: staring, misgendering or uneven hospitality reactions are most plausible in hostels, nightlife and medical encounters, particularly outside the central areas. No local ordinance, facility ban or district-level rule departing from national law is known, and there is no documented local pattern of police targeting, trans-specific violence or service exclusion aimed at visitors; local civic institutions are generally law-abiding, and police and courts remain available if hostility arises. The main local uncertainty is how the national rollback debate filters into everyday attitudes, which can produce administrative awkwardness even absent official hostility. The absence of recorded incidents should not be read as a guarantee of smooth institutional handling if a problem does occur.

regions.name: BEJA
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Portugal's national law in full, with no local exception. Beja is a sparsely populated inland district of the Alentejo, an agrarian interior of small towns with an older and more socially conservative population than Lisbon or Porto, where a visibly transgender visitor is unusual and anonymity is much weaker: staring, curiosity, quiet disapproval, misgendering and awkwardness in rural establishments are the likeliest forms of everyday friction, and being outed in a tight-knit community is easier than in the capital. Specialist trans-affirming services, LGBT community support and experienced professionals are thin outside the major cities, so clinics, police desks and other services may show slower, more cautious or less confident handling, and practical recourse often means travelling to distant urban centres. Local enforcement and attitudes are thinly documented rather than assured; no local ordinance or organized campaign targeting trans visitors characterises the district, and the exposure here is social visibility and uneven professional familiarity rather than state targeting.

regions.name: BRAGA
regions.merged_summary: Braga is subject to Portugal's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. It is a mid-sized city in the north and a historic archdiocesan centre with strong Catholic institutions, giving it a more socially conservative character than Lisbon or Porto, alongside a large university population and growing tourism that moderate the local atmosphere. A smaller visible LGBT infrastructure and the reduced anonymity of a mid-sized city mean a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor may draw more staring, curiosity or conservative disapproval than in the capital or the Algarve — particularly outside the university and tourist core — and faces a higher probability of being recognised or outed. Everyday social friction, rather than legal penalty, is the main local difference. Local policing is generally responsive and the courts and ombudsman mechanisms function normally; no local ordinance, border, facility or detention practice departs from the national position, and no documented pattern of trans-specific targeting, service refusal, extortion or violence against visitors is known in Braga.

regions.name: COIMBRA
regions.merged_summary: Coimbra falls under Portugal's national regime in full, with no local exception. A mid-sized university and tourism city in central Portugal, it has a large student population, a visible LGBT community with local student associations and an annual pride event, and an academic, internationally exposed character that tends toward tolerance. Beyond Lisbon and Porto, central Portugal is somewhat more socially conservative: in smaller towns and everyday encounters a trans visitor may draw more curiosity, staring, misgendering or awkward service moments than in the capital, though this tends to show up as social friction rather than hostility or violence. The city has fewer dedicated trans-specific services than the two largest cities, and smaller-city visibility makes being outed more noticeable. No local rule, police practice, facility restriction or document and border requirement specific to Coimbra is known, and no documented pattern of local targeting or trans-specific incidents distinguishes it from the national picture — local reporting for visitors is thin, so a lack of records should not be read as proof such incidents never happen. Local policing and public services follow national institutions, so an outed visitor here would more plausibly face questioning or misgendering than detention or denial of essential care. The operative uncertainties for a visitor are national rather than regional.

regions.name: FARO
regions.merged_summary:
Faro operates under Portuguese national law in full, with no local exception or regional variation to that regime.

The Algarve is Portugal's most tourism-dependent region: a cosmopolitan coastal economy with a large resident foreign population, visible LGBT tourism and established venues along the coast, a university city in Faro, and English widely spoken across hospitality and health services accustomed to international visitors — which tends to make a mismatched document or a gender-nonconforming appearance unremarkable in resort and urban settings. Away from the resorts, smaller inland and coastal towns have older, more traditional populations where discretion, staring, curiosity or misgendering are likelier than official action; complaint handling and record-keeping there are thinner than in Lisbon, and trans support infrastructure is concentrated in the capital rather than the Algarve. Faro is less metropolitan than Lisbon or Porto, so informal reactions can be more noticeable. Police, courts and medical services function under a rule-of-law system that recognises foreign identity documents, and no documented pattern of police targeting, raids, border screening, detention or anti-trans violence specific to Faro is known. The main residual exposure for a visitor is social awkwardness, document mismatches and variable reception at clinics, with legal recourse available.

regions.name: GUARDA
regions.merged_summary:
Guarda is a small inland district capital in central Portugal, set among rural surroundings and the Serra da Estrela, with an older and more socially conservative population than Lisbon or Porto, small cities such as Guarda and Covilhã (home to a university), lighter tourist traffic and far less visible LGBTQ+ community infrastructure. The region is subject to Portugal's national legal framework in full, with no local exception.

The practical difference for a trans visitor is social and institutional rather than legal. Out or visibly trans, a visitor may draw more staring, curiosity, misgendering and misunderstanding than in the larger cities, and may meet uneven service in hotels, clinics or shops; specialist medical care and support services are thinner locally, so continuity of care is harder to arrange. Informal exclusion from private landlords or employers is a plausible friction point, and if an incident does occur, help and remedies may feel slower and less experienced outside the major urban centres. No local ordinance, police campaign or documented pattern of targeting transgender visitors is known for the district, though the absence of local reporting should not be read as evidence of safety. The pending national bills on legal gender recognition concern residents' own documents and would not affect a visitor's home-issued ID.

regions.name: LEIRIA
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Portugal's national law in full, with no local exception. Leiria is a mid-sized coastal city and district in central Portugal, with tourist traffic around the nearby shrine at Fátima and seaside resorts, but without a large or highly visible trans and LGBT community. Compared with Lisbon or Porto it is less cosmopolitan and more socially traditional and Catholic-influenced, so an outed or visibly trans visitor may encounter more staring, curiosity, awkward misgendering or hesitation from frontline staff, and will find fewer specialist services and community supports. Everyday exposure tends to be social friction rather than confrontation, though rural parts of the district are less predictable and offer less anonymity than the town centre. There is no known Leiria-specific ordinance, curfew, facility restriction or enforcement practice diverging from national law, and police and courts operate under the national framework, with no documented record of transgender visitors being targeted by police, border or facility staff locally. That local record is thin rather than reassuring: the absence of documented incidents reflects limited local documentation, not demonstrated safety, and uneven familiarity among frontline staff means implementation of protections may be inconsistent.

regions.name: LISBOA
regions.merged_summary: Lisbon is subject to Portugal's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. As the capital and largest city, it is the country's most cosmopolitan and tourist-facing urban centre: dense public life, a large tourism economy accustomed to foreign visitors, and English-speaking institutions. It hosts the principal trans and LGBT organisations, Pride events and trans-specific services, and records the largest share of legal gender and name changes in the country, with courts and police functioning for complaints and legal and NGO support based in the city. No Lisbon-specific border, detention or facility restriction is known, and there is no documented pattern of police or service hostility toward trans travellers; everyday exposure centres on ordinary friction — occasional stares, misgendering, or a mismatch between foreign documents and presentation in hotels, banks and airports — rather than targeting. The local social climate is among the most accepting in Portugal, with lighter everyday friction than more conservative rural areas, though institutional discretion still warrants ordinary care, particularly for minors or travellers needing medical support. The pending national rollback of self-declaration concerns residents' recognition procedures rather than visitor-facing rules and has not changed operative safeguards for travellers in Lisbon.

regions.name: PORTALEGRE
regions.merged_summary:
Portugal's national framework applies in Portalegre in full, with no local exception or distinct enforcement regime.

Portalegre is a small, ageing, low-density district in the interior of the Alentejo, near the Spanish border, made up of small towns and countryside rather than any major urban centre. It is more rural, agricultural and socially conservative than Lisbon or Porto, with a traditional Catholic presence, a thin trans community, limited visible LGBT infrastructure or nightlife, and fewer trans-aware and specialist gender-care services, so a visitor has less anonymity and may need to travel farther for support. No district-level restrictions, hostile local ordinances, targeted border checks, police hostility, detention or documented anti-trans violence are known here; policing and courts function normally and bias-motivated assault remains prosecutable, though practical recourse in a district this size is slower and more socially exposed than in a large city. The likely local harm for an outed or visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is social friction — curiosity, staring, misgendering, awkward bureaucracy or uneven service — rather than legal punishment, and a mismatch between documents and presentation tends to draw more attention in close-knit communities. The pending national roll-back affects residents' paperwork rather than a visitor's foreign-issued documents, though it is a climate signal. Absence of local incident reporting should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: PORTO
regions.merged_summary: Porto is subject to Portugal's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Porto is Portugal's second city: a university, port and tourism centre with an established LGBTQ scene — including the GInX venue and the Rua de São Bento/Cândido dos Reis area — an annual Pride march and visible community organisations, giving residents more everyday familiarity with gender diversity than elsewhere in the north. The wider northern region is generally more socially conservative and Catholic than Lisbon, and that contrast can show up outside the central districts as staring, misgendering, occasional service friction or isolated bias, even though state authorities are expected to apply national law. No Porto-specific rule, checkpoint, detention practice or facility restriction has been identified that would make a trans visitor's stay harsher than the national picture, and no documented recent pattern of visitor-targeted violence or police profiling of gender-nonconforming people is known. Porto's public history does include the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in the city, which remains a reference point in national debate; it is a dated, isolated case rather than a present enforcement pattern, but it is evidence the city is not frictionless. The national debate over rolling back self-declaration applies equally here and signals a shifting political climate, without itself changing what a visitor experiences on the ground.

Portuguese courts, police, the Ombudsman and consular channels remain available as recourse, and the pending national parliamentary attempts to change the gender-recognition framework are a country-wide matter rather than a Madeira-specific visitor restriction.

regions.name: VIANA DO CASTELO

It is a small coastal city in the Minho region of northern Portugal, near the Spanish border and centred on a compact pilgrimage town, with a modest tourism-based economy. The local social texture is comparatively traditional and strongly Catholic, and the smaller-city scale means anonymity is lower than in Lisbon or Porto: a visibly trans foreign visitor may draw more staring, misgendering or awkward service interactions, and there are fewer visible trans resources than in the larger cities. Politically, the north is a stronghold for the parties behind the pending national roll-back bills, which can colour the local climate around the debate even though the operative law a visitor encounters has not changed. No local ordinance, enforcement practice, facility rule or documented pattern of police targeting, trans-specific violence or service refusal is known to distinguish the district from the national picture; policing, courts and the tourist economy function normally. The practical local difference is social visibility and reduced access to community support rather than any legal restriction.

regions.name: VILA REAL
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Portugal's national law in full, with no local exception. Vila Real is a small inland regional centre in Trás-os-Montes in the north, seat of a largely rural and older district, with a university campus, festivals and a modest tourism economy that bring some contact with outsiders. Northern Portuguese conservatism, Catholic traditions and dense social networks mean anonymity is limited: a visibly transgender visitor is more likely to meet staring, intrusive curiosity, misgendering or general disapproval than in Lisbon or Porto, and word travels quickly in a small community. Trans-specific services and community infrastructure are thin, with specialist care, advocacy support and larger LGBTQ venues concentrated on the coast and the nearest substantial resources in Porto; distance and smaller local infrastructure may make practical help through national police, courts or the Ombudsman slower, though those routes apply unchanged. No documented pattern of local targeting, police hostility or service denial against transgender travellers is known in Vila Real, and the pending national roll-back concerns residents' legal gender recognition rather than how a visitor's own documents are handled.

regions.name: VISEU
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Portugal's national law in full, with no local exception. Viseu is an inland district capital in central Portugal's Dão wine region — a university town in a largely rural, low-tourism corner of the interior, with an older, more traditional and church-influenced population than Lisbon or Porto. Everyday trans visibility is low, and the city has markedly thinner LGBTQ+ support and advocacy infrastructure than the capital, where specialised services are concentrated; a visibly transgender visitor should expect curious staring, misgendering, occasional intrusive or awkward comment and general social friction rather than organised hostility. Local police, hotel and health staff have little routine experience with trans guests, so mismatched documents may produce slower, more confused handling than in the capital, and a discovery episode may involve awkward bureaucratic friction. National courts, police and complaint mechanisms remain available and function here as elsewhere in the country. No documented Viseu pattern of trans-targeted policing, raids, extortion, detention, service denial or facility exclusion is on record, but that absence is not proof of safety, and no local reporting shows how the ongoing national debate plays out on the ground — uncertainty that should not be read as protection. The 2006 Gisberta killing occurred in Porto and reflects no Viseu-specific pattern.

regions.name: BOQUERON
regions.merged_summary: Boquerón is subject to Paraguay's national law in full, with no local exception. The department is Paraguay's vast, sparsely populated western Chaco, a largely rural and ranching region centred on small towns and conservative Mennonite colonies such as Filadelfia, Neuland and Loma Plata, alongside Indigenous Enxet and other dispersed communities, with limited tourism around Chaco national parks. Its border with Bolivia and Argentina means routine document checks at crossings. No local anti-discrimination ordinance or trans-specific protection is known, and no Boquerón-specific arrest policy, facility restriction or documented targeting of trans visitors is established; that gap is uncertainty, not evidence of safety. Instead, the practical local conditions are the ones that shape how the national regime lands: strongly religious, socially conservative communities with minimal LGBT visibility or community infrastructure; very limited anonymity in small, dispersed settlements where a visibly trans visitor stands out; long distances to Asunción and thin police, legal and health capacity for recourse after an incident. Rural clinics may not consistently apply the national social-name health resolution, and trans-specific advocacy is scarce. The main exposure for a discovered visitor is therefore social hostility, intrusive scrutiny, service friction or delayed and denied care, with ineffective complaints, rather than state-directed arrest. Lower urban nightlife density may reduce some street exposure, but small-town visibility makes discovery difficult to contain.

regions.name: ITAPUA
regions.merged_summary: Itapúa operates under Paraguay's national regime in full, with no local exception. The department is a tourism- and trade-oriented border area: Encarnación sits across the Paraná from Posadas, Argentina, where a visiting trans person can obtain aligned documents and continue care — a practical route Paraguay itself does not offer — while Encarnación's border commerce, hotels and transport flows make passport-and-presentation mismatches a routine possibility at bridges and at police or migration checks. Outside Encarnación the department is more rural and socially conservative than Asunción, with fewer trans-specific services or community supports; conservative religious and agricultural communities, including Mennonite and evangelical enclaves, can intensify social disapproval, and in smaller towns a disclosure can circulate quickly through family, church, employer and school networks. Police and health staff are reported to apply national practice unevenly. No Itapúa-specific hostile legislation, municipal exclusion measure, or documented local pattern of anti-trans violence or police targeting of visitors is known, and no local ordinance adds visitor-facing protections; social friction rather than state threat-framing characterises what an outed visitor can expect. Conditional discovery mainly means misgendering, bureaucratic exposure, possible service refusal or harassment, with little dependable recourse nearby. The lack of recorded local incidents should not be read as protection, and Encarnación's tourism and urban character is not by itself evidence of effective safety.

regions.name: PRESIDENTE HAYES
regions.merged_summary: Presidente Hayes is a sparsely populated Chaco department west of the Paraguay River from Asunción, centred on Villa Hayes and Benjamín Aceval, with small-town social networks, a cattle- and military-present frontier character, religious conservatism and strong machismo norms, and little tolerance for gender nonconformity. The region is subject to Paraguay's national law in full, with no local exception. Health, legal-aid and emergency services are thin and distant, and tourist infrastructure is limited, so the anonymity and practical recourse available in the capital are harder to obtain; adult or family travel raises exposure through clinics, lodging, schools and emergency contacts. Visibility as trans is likelier to draw hostile attention than in Asunción — gossip, staring, service refusal and awkward or discriminatory treatment in clinics, hotels and police encounters, alongside document-marker mismatch at stops — with remedy routed through distant national institutions and local bureaucracy, police and clinics where discretion is wide and follow-through weak. No organised targeting, raids or lethal enforcement against trans visitors is documented locally; the absence of recorded incidents reflects limited local documentation rather than demonstrated protection.

regions.name: Al Daayen
regions.merged_summary: Al Daayen falls wholly under Qatar's national law and national policing, with no local exception or separate legal regime. The municipality covers the northern coastal developments centred on Lusail — a planned, affluent district of high-rise residential towers, malls, hotels and the Lusail Stadium built largely for expatriate residents and international visitors, giving it a mixed, expatriate-heavy and mostly residential, peri-urban character. Its quieter family-oriented retail and beach areas appear to draw less nightlife policing than central Doha, but visible gender nonconformity still attracts official and public attention, and high-profile venues and security operations increase visibility rather than offer protection. Policing, border screening, criminal investigation and detention in the region are carried out by the same national bodies operating elsewhere in Qatar, so a trans visitor discovered here faces the same documented exposure to arrest, custody and removal as in any other part of the country — no local safeguard, sanctuary policy, lesser enforcement or documented local tolerance is known.

regions.name: Al Rayyan
regions.merged_summary:
Al Rayyan is subject to Qatar's national law in full, with no local exception. The municipality sits in Qatar's western urban belt, taking in Education City, Aspire Zone, Villaggio, major event stadia, hotels and universities alongside family suburbs and migrant-labour accommodation. Policing is carried out by national CID and Ministry of Interior officers operating uniformly across the country, and no municipal ordinance, protective practice or local tolerance signal is known to offset state exposure for a trans visitor discovered here.

The area's character can raise rather than lower visibility. Family-oriented, high-visibility malls and surveillance at prominent visitor venues concentrate public scrutiny, and enforcement has reached visitors around high-profile events. Al Rayyan's large Filipino, Indonesian and Thai migrant population includes communities documented as specially targeted in post-2022 police operations, adding discovery risk. The district's cosmopolitan, expatriate and tourism-facing surroundings may offer ordinary discretion in private spaces, but this is not a protection: public policing continues, and family or school-related inquiries can bring state and guardian pressure. No local protection or effective remedy specific to trans visitors is documented.

regions.name: Umm Slal
regions.merged_summary: Umm Slal falls fully under Qatar's national legal regime, with no local exception. Umm Slal is a largely residential municipality north of Doha, with traditional family neighbourhoods, a conservative social fabric and little visitor-facing infrastructure. No local evidence was found distinguishing how that regime operates here from the national picture — no separate local policing practice, no documented local protection or shelter, and no known LGBT-friendly venue or advocacy service where a trans visitor could seek help. The absence of local reporting should not be read as safety; how local authorities would actually act remains uncertain rather than reassuring.

regions.name: ARGES
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception. Argeș county is centred on Pitești and combines small industrial towns with rural, largely Orthodox communities that are generally more socially conservative and less familiar with transgender people than major cities such as Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Brașov or Timișoara. The county has no Pride event, no specialist LGBT centre or legal-aid service, and its smaller towns offer far less anonymity than the big cities, so a visitor whose documents and presentation do not match may face staring, invasive questioning, misgendering, refusal of informal services at hotels, clinics or police counters, and family or community pressure if identity is disclosed, with no accessible local remedy. No Argeș-specific enforcement, policing, border or document-check practice, local protective ordinance or documented police targeting over presentation is known; national police practice and the courts govern, and courts remain a functioning recourse. Organised confrontation of the kind seen elsewhere in Romania has no Argeș counterpart, so exposure here is more likely to be social friction than state targeting.

regions.name: BACAU
regions.merged_summary: Bacău is subject to Romania's national legal framework in full, with no local exception, and no regional law, facility rule or documented incident targeting trans visitors is known. What differs is local texture: Bacău is a mid-sized city in eastern Romania's Moldavia region, strongly Orthodox and socially conservative, with no recorded Pride event and no visible local trans or LGBT community infrastructure. Specialist legal and advocacy support is thinner than in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Brașov or Timișoara, so a visibly trans visitor is more conspicuous there, and requests for help or complaints would most plausibly be routed through national bodies. Everyday exposure rests on social climate rather than state action: mismatched papers at hotels, banks, clinics or during police checks, uncomfortable questioning or misgendering, staring, gossip and possible delay or refusal of routine services, including health care, with harassment reports potentially handled perfunctorily. In any custodial situation, placement would default to birth sex. Ordinary travel, hotels and public transport remain available without trans-specific restrictions, no organised targeting is known, and national courts and EU-level safeguards continue to apply.

regions.name: BRASOV
regions.merged_summary:
Brașov is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception.

Brașov is a university and tourism-oriented city in Transylvania, and its visitor economy — hotels, clinics, transport desks, banks and official identity checks — is where a mismatch between presentation and documents is most likely to surface. Social attitudes are mixed, and the city is generally more conservative than Bucharest, so an outed visitor may meet stares, misgendering, service friction or harassment, with police recourse that is uneven in practice rather than hostile by rule; Orthodox conservatism and national right-wing hostility to LGBTI visibility form the backdrop. Emergency or medical care may be uneven if staff are unfamiliar with trans needs. No local ordinance, police sweep, facility regime or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors has been documented here, and no region-specific protective legislation covers visitors — this absence of local evidence should not be read as safety, and local custody and facility practice is not documented. Pride activity in the city has served as limited positive evidence about public events only, not a guide to accommodation, clinics or late-night streets.

regions.name: CLUJ
regions.merged_summary:
Cluj-Napoca, the main city of Cluj county in Transylvania, is Romania's leading university and technology centre, with a large student and foreign-resident population, an active queer community and a widely held reputation as one of the country's more tolerant places; the region is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception. The city's Pride events proceeded without incidents in 2025, unlike the attempted bans and heavy policing seen in other Romanian cities, and police and public services locally appear more accustomed to diversity than in the county's rural areas, which remain more conservative.

In practice, a trans visitor is more likely to face bureaucratic confusion, staring, misgendering, occasional harassment or service friction than police action. Local administration has shown institutional conservatism on documents: Cluj civil-status directorates were among the bodies that appealed the 2026 ruling ordering transcription of an EU-issued gender recognition, so mismatched ID can still create friction with local services. No Cluj-specific targeting of trans visitors, facility restrictions or adverse treatment of foreign documents is documented — that reflects a lack of records rather than an assurance of safety, and remedies for gender-identity discrimination remain weak.

regions.name: DAMBOVITA
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Romania's national regime in full, with no local exception. Dâmbovișta is a predominantly small-town and rural county centred on Târgoviște, with strong Orthodox cultural influence and less everyday familiarity with trans visitors than in Bucharest or western cities, so social friction such as staring or misgendering may be more noticeable if a visitor is clocked. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Dâmbovița from the national picture; the national regime, including its protections and their limits, is what applies here.

regions.name: MARAMURES
regions.merged_summary:
Maramureș is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a largely rural region of the north-west centred on Baia Mare and Sighetu Marmației, with village guesthouse tourism around Bârsana, Săpânța, the wooden churches and the open-air village museums. It is deeply Orthodox and Greek-Catholic, with preserved customary social norms, and outside its small towns a visibly transgender visitor has little anonymity: curiosity, staring, misgendering and gossip are plausible, and in family-run lodging, hospitality or local clinics an unusual presentation or an identity-document mismatch can bring intrusive questions, delays or a refusal of service — guesthouses, hotels, clinics and transport services routinely check documents. Local civil-society and legal-aid support is thin, with greater distance from Bucharest-based organisations than in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca or Timișoara, and no Pride event or trans-specific local body is documented in the county.

Set against that, Maramureș is an established international tourism destination where foreign visitors are routine, and tourist-facing businesses generally avoid confrontation, so unusual presentation tends to read as an oddity rather than a spectacle. No region-specific record of violence, organised targeting, hostile local legislation or enforcement practice against transgender visitors has been documented, and no local rule differs from the national picture; the chief exposure after discovery is social hostility and practical service friction rather than arrest or state action. The absence of documented local incidents is not an assurance of safety, and how a particular situation would be handled locally remains uncertain.

regions.name: PRAHOVA
regions.merged_summary: Prahova County is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception. Locally the county pairs the industrial centre of Ploiești and conservative, Orthodox-influenced rural areas with the tourism-dependent Prahova Valley resorts of Sinaia, Bușteni and Azuga. There is little queer infrastructure, and no local ordinance, checkpoint or documented police campaign against trans visitors has been identified; any official recourse a visitor might seek runs through institutions based in Bucharest. Everyday exposure is more likely to be social than state: staring, misgendering, intrusive questioning about documents, and possible refusal of service in shops, venues or private services. The resort economy, geared to visitors, tends toward discreet customer-service handling, which can lower friction in hotels and mountain venues, while Ploiești and the surrounding countryside are less accustomed to gender-nonconforming travellers. The tourist-facing valley towns are likelier to be merely impersonal than hostile. Nothing local points to systematic official targeting of trans visitors; where serious problems arise, they follow national patterns of documentation and procedure rather than any Prahova-specific rule.

regions.name: SATU MARE
regions.merged_summary: Satu Mare operates in full under Romania's national legal framework, with no local exception. Satu Mare is a county and small city in Romania's north-west, on the Ukrainian and Hungarian borders, that is largely rural, socially conservative and religiously observant, with a large Hungarian-speaking minority. Compared with Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca or Timișoara it has far less visible LGBTQ+ infrastructure: no Pride event, LGBT organisation or visible trans community is documented locally, and no police hate-crime training for the area is on record — so complaints, referrals and support travel farther and institutional follow-through is thinner than in the capital. No local pattern of police targeting, trans-specific violence, facility bans, or border, custody or health-care rules reaching travellers is documented; national anti-discrimination channels remain available but are distant and slow here. In practice, a visibly trans visitor is more conspicuous, and most likely to encounter staring, misgendering, invasive curiosity, service hesitation and awkward hotel or ID checks rather than arrest. Hotels and police are not recorded as actively hostile, but local recourse, medical and police familiarity with trans issues, and support services are thin, and bureaucratic corrections move more slowly outside the capital. Ordinary interactions reflect a mixed climate of tolerance and discomfort, and the border and minority setting adds no distinct trans-specific exposure beyond that.

regions.name: TIMIS
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Romania's national law in full, with no local exception. Timiș County, in Romania's west, is centred on Timișoara, a multicultural Banat city with a large university and a significant IT sector, a historically cosmopolitan outlook and a visible civic and LGBT community; it was European Capital of Culture in 2023. Pride events in Timișoara have proceeded without incidents, in contrast to the attempted municipal ban on Oradea Pride, and urban institutions there generally respond predictably to visitors, including foreign ones. Everyday exposure for a trans visitor is more likely to be social friction, misgendering or bureaucratic and service friction where identity documents conflict with presentation than any organised hostility: no local ordinance, facility restriction, or documented pattern of police or public targeting specific to Timiș is known, and that lack of documented incidents should not be read as proof of safety. Conditions are uneven across the county — the surrounding rural areas are more socially conservative than the city, and visitors should expect the greatest ease in Timișoara itself rather than generalising the city's atmosphere to the whole county. Institutional follow-through on gender-identity claims is limited nationwide, so remedies exist but may be slow in practice.

regions.name: Chuvashia
regions.merged_summary: Chuvashia is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. The republic is a largely rural, socially conservative Volga region centred on Cheboksary, where a visibly trans visitor would find little anonymity outside the capital and where no queer-friendly venues, advocacy groups or local protective policies are documented. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Chuvashia from the national picture in how these rules reach a trans visitor, so the country-level regime as stated governs here. The absence of recorded local incidents should not be read as safety, and uncertainty about how or how often federal powers are exercised in the republic is not a form of protection.

regions.name: Kaluga Oblast
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Kaluga Oblast from the national picture — there are no documented local protections, exceptions, or known harsher enforcement, and the absence of local reports does not establish safety. Kaluga is a smaller, more conservative provincial oblast than Moscow or St Petersburg, without documented LGBT community infrastructure or safe venues, and its regional institutions operate under the same federal authorities that conduct raids and extremism prosecutions. A trans visitor outed there faces the same federal enforcement, social exposure, and absence of recourse documented nationally.

regions.name: Lipetsk Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Lipetsk Oblast is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. The oblast is a conservative industrial and agricultural region with no known trans-specific services, visible queer infrastructure, or local protections, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor may draw attention with little anonymity or advocacy support. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Lipetsk Oblast from the national picture — there are no recorded local protections, sanctuary practices, or softened enforcement patterns, and the absence of known local incidents should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Russia's national regime in full, with no local exception or documented local mitigation.

Nenets Autonomous Okrug is a sparsely populated Arctic district of roughly 44,000 people centred on Naryan-Mar, reachable mainly by air, with outlying oil and gas settlements and traditional hunting and reindeer-herding communities with a large indigenous Nenets population. Federal police and courts enforce national law here directly, but the okrug has no LGBTQ venues, no community or support organisations, and no local legal aid; healthcare and police services are limited. Social attitudes are conservative, and in small, close-knit settlements a visibly transgender outsider draws attention rather than the anonymity a large city might offer, with less institutional buffering than Moscow or St. Petersburg. The practical difference from the national picture is reduced privacy, fewer places to go and less recourse if trouble arises — not a milder outcome: a trans visitor who is discovered faces the same exposure to official scrutiny as elsewhere in Russia, and bias-motivated violence carries neither protection nor aggravating weight. No documented local protection, complaint mechanism or sanctuary exists to offset that exposure, and nothing local should be read as evidence of greater safety.

regions.name: Novgorod Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Novgorod Oblast is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. The local colour that does exist is limited: Veliky Novgorod is a small, socially conservative provincial city where a visibly trans visitor is conspicuous to police, hotel staff and strangers, and where the queer venue and support scene is far thinner than in Moscow or St Petersburg. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing the oblast from the national picture — there is no local protective law, tolerance exception, or documented pattern of either harsher or softer enforcement on record. Absence of local incident reports should not be read as safety: passport checks, police stops and custody proceed under federal authority, and the city's heritage tourism economy offers no documented shield.

regions.name: Oryol Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Oryol Oblast lies in central Russia and is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is an interior, socially conservative oblast with no significant tourism-facing economy, no known trans-specific protections or community infrastructure, and smaller cities where a visibly trans visitor has little anonymity. Beyond this general character, no region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Oryol Oblast from the national picture in protective law, police practice, access to services or documented local tolerance — nothing local has been recorded that either softens or sharpens the conditions described at country level, so those conditions should be treated as operating here unchanged.

regions.name: Primorsky Krai
regions.merged_summary:
Primorsky Krai is subject to Russia's national law and security practices in full, with no local exception or deviation.

Vladivostok, the krai's main city, is a major Pacific port with a history of cross-border tourism and a tourist core that is somewhat more cosmopolitan than the Far East interior; a small underground queer scene has existed there. That however is thin cover: the region has no documented local protections, sanctuary measures, or identity-respecting police, health, or facility protocols, and as a peripheral Far East centre it offers little visible trans support infrastructure or consistent institutional recourse. The krai is a militarised border region with conservative authorities, and border and port screening adds real discovery risk — document and presentation mismatches can draw scrutiny at ports, checkpoints, hotel registration, and routine police stops. Police oversight in the Far East is reported as weaker than in the European centres, and nationalist violence against gender-nonconforming people has a local record. Social attitudes across the krai remain broadly hostile. Limited local reporting does not establish that enforcement is absent or lighter here; a trans visitor found out in Primorsky Krai faces the same custody, prosecution, and detention environment as elsewhere in the country, which carries documented lethal risk.

regions.name: Sakhalin Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Sakhalin Oblast is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. Nothing found here distinguishes the oblast from the national picture: no local protective measure, no more tolerant local climate, and no distinct enforcement practice has been documented for Sakhalin, and that silence should not be read as safety. The oblast is a remote, sparsely populated island province with limited nightlife and small ferry, port and air links to the mainland and Japan, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor may stand out more than in a large metropolis. Federal courts, security services and registration systems operate throughout the oblast, so national enforcement reaches the islands as it does anywhere else in the country.

regions.name: Smolensk Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Smolensk Oblast is subject to Russia's national legal regime in full, with no local exception or documented mitigation. The oblast is a conservative western region adjoining Belarus, made up of modest-size cities and towns with limited visible LGBTQ infrastructure, where a foreign visitor stands out more than in a large metropolitan centre. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Smolensk Oblast from the national picture — and the absence of local records of incidents, protections or enforcement exceptions should not be read as indicating safer conditions.

regions.name: Tver Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Tver Oblast is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. Tver is a conservative central Russian province on the Moscow–Petersburg corridor, with little visible queer infrastructure outside limited urban venues. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Tver Oblast from the national picture — no local protections, distinct enforcement pattern, or separate treatment of trans visitors has been documented — so local conditions should not be assumed either more protective or more punitive than the country-level description.

regions.name: Tyumen Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Tyumen Oblast is subject to Russia's national regime in full, with no local exception or protective measure. Locally, the oblast is a prosperous oil-and-gas province: Tyumen city is a major Siberian urban centre with a university population that can offer some everyday anonymity, while much of the surrounding territory is rural. Social attitudes here run more conservative than in Moscow or St Petersburg, trans visibility is low, and organised LGBTQ venues, advocacy networks and trans-specific visitor resources are limited or absent; no regional ordinance, sanctuary practice or local protection is documented. The oblast's large, partly rural geography and its distance from legal-aid centres in Moscow and St Petersburg mean that a trans visitor stopped or outed by police has little practical recourse. Federal and local officers retain discretion in enforcement, and the region's oil-industrial character brings general stability and monitoring but no trans-specific safeguards. A visitor discovered as transgender faces the national exposure, with no local remedy.

regions.name: Red Sea
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sudan's national law in full, with no local exception. Port Sudan is the country's main maritime and air gateway and, since 2023, the army-held seat of government, so state institutions — police, courts and morality enforcement — operate directly there rather than leaving a gap in authority; visitors face repeated border and security checks where mismatched documents or visible presentation can trigger questioning, secondary screening or referral to the police. The city's large humanitarian and diplomatic presence, functioning airports, and limited tourism around Suakin and Red Sea diving sites give foreigners modest anonymity and better consular access than elsewhere in Sudan, but this does not amount to protection. Local society in the coastal state is conservative, with strong Beja tribal and Sunni religious norms, Sufi-rooted authority, little public tolerance for gender diversity, and no documented local LGBT community infrastructure or protective structures. Wartime displacement and the conflict's focus on border control have strained policing and courts without creating any local record of softer enforcement or relief; no region-specific evidence of more favourable treatment than the national picture is known.

regions.name: West Darfur
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Sudan's national law in full, with no local exception. West Darfur has been at the centre of armed conflict since 2023, with the Rapid Support Forces and allied militias exercising de facto control across much of the region, fighting concentrated around the regional capital and displacement camps, and ethnically targeted violence documented alongside near-total impunity. Policing and courts have effectively collapsed: there are no functioning complaint mechanisms, and checkpoints, ID checks and armed-group scrutiny of strangers make discovery of a visitor's documents or presentation unusually likely. In that setting, arrest under national provisions is only one of the risks — arbitrary detention, extortion, beating, sexualised assault and lethal violence by armed actors enforcing conservative norms informally are documented in the region's ad hoc facilities and settlements, with no realistic recourse or consular protection. Social conservatism, the rural character of much of the area, and the absence of any protective civil society or tourist infrastructure leave no safe reporting route, and conflict has further narrowed access to gender-affirming and emergency care. No region-specific pattern of arrests targeting trans people, border practices or facility rules is documented, and no route to execution on the basis of trans identity is established — but neither is any effective protection, and the undocumented gaps are not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Diourbel
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Senegal's national law in full, with no local exception. Diourbel contains Touba, the Mouride spiritual centre, and its society is among the most religiously conservative and closely supervised in the country. Public life is shaped by religious authority, dress and comportment are policed by the community, and denunciation to police is common; a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner attracts conspicuous attention, with local institutions and crowds unlikely to offer protection if discovered. The anonymity available in Dakar does not apply here: Diourbel is more rural, with weaker tourist-facing infrastructure, stronger local religious authority and less international visibility, and rural settings have historically produced extralegal violence against people outed as LGBT elsewhere in Senegal. LGBT people in the region keep an extremely low profile, and no local protective mechanism, queer community infrastructure, or independent complaint mechanism is documented. Police and neighbourhood reporting pressures apply with at least equal force here, and enforcement is expected to be discretionary and socially amplified, with detention, prosecution, extortion and community hostility all plausible for a visitor who is discovered. No distinct local enforcement record distinguishing Diourbel from the national picture has been documented, and the absence of such a record should not be read as evidence of greater safety; religious and community authority does not replace or soften national law.

regions.name: Kaffrine
regions.merged_summary: Kaffrine is subject to Senegal's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is an inland, predominantly rural agricultural area far from Dakar and its international gateway, with little tourism-facing infrastructure and few of the advocacy, legal-aid or consular channels available in the capital. Its small, tight-knit communities offer far less anonymity than the city, and local religious and social disapproval of LGBT people is strong, so outing or discovery carries immediate practical consequences; police and gendarmerie may act on community reports rather than formal complaints, leaving little recourse when intervention occurs. There is no visible local LGBT community infrastructure and no known protective measure, local exception or distinct visitor-facing practice for transgender travellers. No Kaffrine-specific incident pattern is documented — the absence of regional reports reflects sparse reporting outside Dakar rather than evidence of safety.

regions.name: Kaolack
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Senegal's national law in full, with no local exception. Kaolack is a major central city and a prominent religious centre — conservative, closely knit and socially watchful, so anonymity is limited for anyone whose gender presentation draws attention. It is not a tourist destination, and no local organisations, services or other protective infrastructure for trans visitors are documented. In October 2023, the body of Cheikh Fall, a man outed as gay, was exhumed and burned in a street in Kaolack before a crowd of hundreds; four suspected organisers were apprehended days later, though their prosecution is not documented. The case shows how quickly a suspicion of same-sex conduct can escalate into public, collective violence here, well beyond official channels, with informal reporting and community scrutiny raising the chance of exposure. Police and courts are described as reflecting prevailing hostility, offering little effective remedy if a trans visitor is detained, denied services or attacked. Kaolack has no documented local tolerance offsetting these conditions, and no trans-specific incident involving a visitor has been recorded in the region.

regions.name: Kolda
regions.merged_summary: Kolda is subject to Senegal's national regime in full, with no local exception. The region is a largely rural southern part of Casamance, bordering Guinea-Bissau and lying close to The Gambia, with a predominantly Muslim and Fulani population, very few foreign visitors, limited tourism infrastructure, and far fewer services or support networks than Dakar. Socially it is conservative and tightly knit: a transgender visitor whose status became known would be highly visible, and word would travel quickly through family, neighbourhood and religious networks, raising the likelihood of denunciation. Police and legal aid are thinner than in the capital, anonymity is scarce, and customary and religious authority carries strong weight, so an outsider has little practical recourse. Border and transport checks add exposure, since a mismatch in presented documents can trigger secondary screening, and the Guinea-Bissau frontier also serves as a potential exit route. No local tolerance mechanism, protective institution, or support structure that would soften national conditions for a trans visitor is documented in the region.

regions.name: Sedhiou
regions.merged_summary: Sédhiou is a small, rural town in lower Casamance where a foreign visitor stands out, community gossip travels quickly, and routine identity checks or border-adjacent movement can compound the chance of being reported. The region is subject to Senegal's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Sédhiou from the national picture: no local protective measures, tolerance regime, or documented local incidents are known, and these gaps do not establish safety. Limited anonymity, thin advocacy infrastructure, and strong social scrutiny mean a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor should assume exposure to the national conditions applies, with little effective remedy if outed.

regions.name: CENTRAL REGION
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Singapore's national law in full, with no local exception. The Central Region is the island's densely urban, commercial and visitor-facing core — Orchard, Marina Bay, Bugis, the Suntec convention district and Hong Lim Park, where the annual Pink Dot gathering is held — packed with international hotels, transport nodes and event venues, and staffed by professional service workers accustomed to foreign guests. Everyday interaction here is comparatively cosmopolitan and tourist-facing, a visible LGBTQ nightlife and venue scene operates, and policing is orderly and non-violent, with dense CCTV and rapid response. Against that, no local law, facility rule or enforcement practice adds protection beyond the national picture: document checks at hotels, immigration counters and convention venues are routine, and a mismatch between papers and presentation can bring bureaucratic questioning, misgendering or possible refusal of accommodation rather than arrest. Gender-neutral facilities are scarce in the district's hotels and venues, and organised public objection to them has surfaced locally, so social friction rather than institutional hostility is the more likely difficulty. No local record of targeted violence against trans visitors or police profiling of transgender tourists is documented, though the absence of such reports should not be read as a guarantee; formal recourse for service refusal remains thin, and outcomes in individual cases are uncertain.

regions.name: EAST REGION
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Singapore's national law in full, with no local exception. The East Region covers Changi, Tampines, Bedok, Pasir Ris and the East Coast Park area, and Changi Airport — the country's main entry point — sits within it alongside nearby checkpoints. Screening there is orderly and procedurally bound, and no region-specific targeting or special screening practice for trans visitors is known: a mismatch between documents and presentation may prompt secondary questioning or bureaucratic friction rather than detention as policy.

Away from the airport belt the region is largely HDB heartland with conservative Chinese and Malay communities, where a visibly trans visitor is more likely to draw stares, misgendering or service awkwardness than confrontation. Public toilets and changing facilities remain a point of friction, and any custody or hospital encounter would likely be arranged by recorded sex. Police and courts are professional and rule-of-law based, so exposure here falls well short of violence or imprisonment because of gender presentation — but no East Region-specific protection mitigates the limits of the national framework, and practical recourse for discrimination or intrusive questioning remains thin.

regions.name: NORTH REGION
regions.merged_summary: North Region falls under Singapore's national regime in full, with no separate local law, ordinance or enforcement practice of its own. What sets it apart is social and geographic texture rather than legal exposure: this is heartland Singapore — Woodlands, Yishun, Sembawang, Admiralty and neighbouring HDB towns — a largely residential area with no tourism or nightlife infrastructure, no queer venues or community organisations of its own, and fewer gender-neutral facilities than the central districts. The resident profile includes a large Malay-Muslim population, and familiarity with visibly gender-diverse people is lower than in central areas, so a trans visitor who is noticed may meet staring, curiosity, misgendering, awkward questions or some service friction rather than confrontation; local accounts describe conservatism expressed as disapproval rather than violence, and there is no record of organised targeting here, though that reflects a lack of documented cases rather than any local protection. The region's main document encounter is Woodlands Checkpoint, the land crossing to Johor Bahru, where routine passport checks make a mismatch between presentation and recorded sex more likely to draw secondary questioning, delay or entry difficulty than at the airport. Public facilities here remain largely binary.

regions.name: NORTH-EAST REGION
regions.merged_summary: The North-East Region is subject to Singapore's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a dense residential heartland of HDB new towns — Ang Mo Kio, Hougang, Serangoon, Sengkang and Punggol — away from the central tourist belt, so everyday interactions occur in neighbourhood malls, clinics and MRT stations rather than tourist or nightlife settings. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture: no local law, enforcement pattern, or documented treatment of trans visitors differs from what is described at country level, and no record of local tolerance beyond the national norm exists either. Absence of such local evidence should not be read as a guarantee of safety; where local practice is undocumented, it remains unknown rather than reassuring.

regions.name: WEST REGION
regions.merged_summary: The West Region is part of Singapore's unified national system, with no separate local law, border regime or enforcement authority, so the national regime applies in full. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this area from the national picture. The West is largely HDB residential heartland and industrial land — Jurong, Bukit Batok, Choa Chu Kang, Tuas, along with the NTU and NUS corridor — with few LGBT-specific venues and a socially conservative everyday climate, so routine administrative encounters such as document, bathroom or lodging checks may feel less practised than in the centre; how local officials or venues handle a particular document mismatch or facility question is undocumented and should not be assumed safe.

regions.name: Choiseul
regions.merged_summary: Choiseul is subject to Solomon Islands national law in full, with no local exception. The province is remote and sparsely populated, with negligible tourism infrastructure, no visible trans community and no LGBT organisation. Social discipline is carried largely by customary chiefs and by Anglican, Catholic and Adventist churches, and in small village settings there is very little anonymity — anyone read as gender-nonconforming is likely to become known quickly through local networks rather than through formal checks. Policing and courts are thin outside the provincial centre, so a visitor who is outed would more plausibly face communal responses — shaming, hostile questioning, pressure to leave — than documented state action, and distant police, medical and consular help offer little practical recourse. Any detention would be at birth sex with no trans-specific safeguards. No province-specific records of trans-directed violence, detention or enforcement were found; these expectations rest on rurality and governance structure rather than on recorded incidents, and the thin local evidence base should not be read as evidence of safety. Isolation reduces routine contact with officials, but the absence of local support services or remedy means discovery carries consequences with no institutional recourse beyond church and custom, and remedy is thinner than in Honiara.

regions.name: Rennell and Bellona
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Solomon Islands national law in full, with no local exception. Rennell and Bellona is a remote outer-island province of a few thousand residents — a small, overwhelmingly church-going Polynesian society governed socially by clergy and chiefs, with Anglican, Seventh-day Adventist and South Seas Evangelical congregations and strong church and customary authority. Villages are tight-knit and every stranger becomes known within days, so a transgender visitor is highly conspicuous and outing would spread quickly through local networks, risking social hostility, exclusion, service refusal or pressure with little institutional recourse. Formal capacity is thin: minimal police presence, limited medical facilities, no local advocacy or complaint mechanism, no police training or health infrastructure for gender diversity, and no trans-specific protective machinery — practical help generally requires travel to Honiara. Ecotourism brings some foreign visitors, but tourism volume is very low. There is no documented local record of trans-specific policing, raids, violence or prosecutions, nor of acceptance; this reflects an absence of local evidence rather than demonstrated safety. Detention, if it occurred, would likely mean small local cells and a delayed official response. Remoteness reduces the likelihood of official attention, but it equally reduces a visitor's options if hostility arises.

regions.name: Temotu
regions.merged_summary: Temotu is subject to Solomon Islands national law in full, with no local exception. Temotu is the country's remote easternmost province, centred on Lata in the scattered Santa Cruz Islands: small, dispersed communities with almost no tourism infrastructure, minimal policing and medical capacity, no consular presence and no resident advocacy organisations. Thin transport links and limited visitor services mean that reaching help or leaving quickly in a difficulty is hard, and in villages where everyone knows everyone, disputes tend to be settled informally, leaving a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner with little realistic recourse, legal aid or discreet services nearby. Strong customary and church-centred social influence shapes local expectations, and an openly gender-diverse visitor would be conspicuous at once, raising exposure to outing, community pressure, stigmatised questioning, accommodation or service exclusion, and slow response rather than any documented targeting by authorities. Against that, Melanesian culture recognises gender-variant roles such as akavaine, general hospitality toward visitors is high, and no Temotu-specific violence, border targeting or police attention toward trans visitors appears in the record — so local conditions add friction and thin recourse rather than a distinct local policy. The absence of recorded targeting is not proof of safety.

regions.name: Western
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Solomon Islands' national law in full, with no local exception. Centered on Gizo and the Marovo Lagoon and taking in New Georgia, Ranongga, Choiseul and Munda, Western Province is largely rural and remote, with services and administrative presence concentrated in Gizo and Munda. Its dive-resort and tourism economy around Gizo, Marovo Lagoon and Munda brings regular expatriate contact, so foreign guests are generally accommodated and a visibly transgender visitor tends to go unremarked in tourist-facing settings; everyday reactions there run from curiosity to conservative disapproval rather than organised hostility, and there is no provincial record of police targeting gender-nonconforming travellers. Against that, church congregations and village or chiefly authority carry strong social weight, and small, closely knit island communities offer little anonymity: a visitor who is discovered is more likely to face gossip, staring, refusal of service, exclusion or pressure from hosts than formal arrest, particularly outside the tourism centres, with limited privacy in guesthouses, clinics and transport. Provincial police and courts are thinly resourced, so service denial or harassment would leave little practical recourse. Health facilities are basic and offer no trans-specific care, and anything beyond routine treatment requires referral to Honiara. Documentation of trans visitors specifically in the province is sparse, so the local picture rests partly on general knowledge of conditions — and thin local records should not be read as protection.

regions.name: Western Area
regions.merged_summary: Western Area, centred on Freetown, is subject to Sierra Leone's national law in full, with no local exception. It is the country's capital, main port and principal tourism hub, with beach resorts, hotels, a diplomatic quarter, universities and a dense concentration of NGOs, media and humanitarian staff. That international presence, together with urban anonymity, modestly softens everyday scrutiny compared with rural districts, and social attitudes are reported as somewhat more moderate than in the provinces. Official practice does not follow: the capital concentrates police checkpoints, patrols and the security apparatus, and passport, hotel and presentation checks are routine, so gender nonconformity or a document mismatch is more likely to be noticed here than in remote areas. Crowded markets and transport hubs add to that exposure, and strongly conservative public attitudes remain operative, meaning visible gender nonconformity can draw stops, detention or public humiliation. No local sanctuary policy, protective ordinance or trans-specific enforcement data is documented. Freetown's NGO and civil-society density can make advice, clinics and embassies easier to reach, but nothing in the local record shows this preventing police mistreatment. The 2004 killing of activist FannyAnn Eddy took place in the capital, a reminder that lethal violence has occurred here. Some evidence is dated, and no distinct Western Area enforcement pattern that would clearly lower visitor risk has been identified.

regions.name: Departamento de Usulután
regions.merged_summary:
Usulután is subject to El Salvador's national legal regime in full, with no local exception.

The department is rural and socially conservative — in the east and southeast — with small towns where a visibly trans outsider draws attention rather than anonymity, and with social environments marked by high religiosity and machismo. It has beaches and small-scale surf tourism, but little tourism overall and little trans-specific infrastructure: legal-aid, NGO and LGBT organisational coverage is thinner than in San Salvador, local authorities, hospitals and security forces offer no known protocols or reliable complaint route, and trans-competent health care is limited outside the capital, so a visitor needing care or medication refills has fewer alternatives. Security forces are heavily present in border and anti-gang operations, and gang activity has been significant in parts of the department, with LGBT people there exposed to extortion, sexual assault and forced recruitment; the mass raids of the state of exception reduced some street-level exposure but left the custodial pathway intact. Practical consequences for a discovered trans visitor include questioning or refusal at lodging, checkpoints or clinics, and, if detained, placement in male facilities with risks of humiliation, extortion and violence. Community or gang hostility in small-town settings is a further danger, and no documented local tolerance, tourist-facing protection or practice by which police or courts have worked for trans people distinguishes Usulután favourably. Foreign status may reduce visibility somewhat but does not offset these consequences, and local incidents are poorly documented, so conditions may differ from what is recorded.

regions.name: Acquaviva
regions.merged_summary: Acquaviva is one of San Marino's nine castelli — a quiet, western hillside municipality taking in the Gualdicciolo area, residential in character, adjoining the capital and close to the Italian border, with no tourism-facing infrastructure or policing of its own. The region is subject to San Marino's national law in full, with no local exception. In a locality this small and socially familiar, a trans visitor who is recognised may meet ordinary curiosity or misgendering, and recourse for identity-related friction is thin, though no local pattern of violence, denial of care or state-directed outing is recorded. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Acquaviva from the national picture.

regions.name: Borgo Maggiore
regions.merged_summary: Borgo Maggiore is San Marino's second-largest municipality, a residential and tourist gateway linked to the capital by cable car and home to the state hospital, where no visitor-specific ward rule is documented. The region is subject to San Marino's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes the municipality from the national picture: it has no separate border, residency, identification, policing or public-facility regime, and no local ordinance or documented practice targets gender-nonconforming visitors — though it also offers no distinct local protective exception.

regions.name: Chiesanuova
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to San Marino's national law in full, with no local exception. Chiesanuova is a small, rural, close-knit residential castello on the Italian border with limited tourist infrastructure and no police or enforcement separate from the national forces, so visibility in such a tiny community is a matter of social friction rather than documented hostility; ordinary social discomfort or service difficulty is the more plausible concern than any local targeting. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Chiesanuova from the national picture.

regions.name: Città di San Marino
regions.merged_summary: Città di San Marino is subject to San Marino's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. No local conditions were found that distinguish the city from the national picture: local policing practice, treatment of a trans visitor, and any remedies for identity-motivated incidents are not documented separately, and the absence of recorded local incidents should not be read as an assurance. As a compact, heavily touristed old-town centre within a small, traditionally minded community, the more plausible everyday friction for a trans visitor is social — curiosity, stares or service awkwardness — rather than official, though formal recourse for identity-based harm remains thinner here than for orientation-based harm.

regions.name: Domagnano
regions.merged_summary: Domagnano is subject to San Marino's national law in full, with no local exception. It is one of the country's nine castelli: a small, quiet residential hill town near the Italian border, closely knit and Catholic-influenced, where everyday discretion and courtesy vary and where being recognised as trans could draw social stigma or minor administrative awkwardness in a compact community, though no pattern of local hostility is recorded. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Domagnano from the national picture for a trans visitor — there is no recorded checkpoint practice, facility or accommodation rule, or enforcement pattern there, and local social attitudes remain undocumented rather than established.

regions.name: Faetano
regions.merged_summary: Faetano is one of San Marino's nine castelli and is subject to San Marino's national regime in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Faetano from the national picture for a trans visitor. Locally it is a small, sparsely populated rural hill village of roughly a thousand people with an agricultural and small-workshop economy and no tourist infrastructure of its own, so a visibly trans traveller stands out and draws curiosity rather than institutional attention. Nothing locally recorded adds a hostile layer — no local ordinance, police targeting, or registry practice reaching guests — but equally there is no trans community or advocacy presence nearby and no dedicated recourse short of national channels, leaving everyday friction or a service refusal largely unremedied.

regions.name: Montegiardino
regions.merged_summary: Montegiardino is one of San Marino's nine castelli, a small rural hillside commune of a few hundred residents that also hosts the University of San Marino, and the region is subject to San Marino's national law in full, with no local exception. Nothing distinguishes Montegiardino from the national picture described at country level, and the lack of local detail should not be read as evidence that conditions here are better or worse than those recorded nationally. In a commune of this size a visitor's presence is more noticeable, but no local rule, checkpoint practice or policing pattern is documented that differs from the national regime.

regions.name: Serravalle
regions.merged_summary: Serravalle falls squarely under San Marino's national regime in full, with no local exception. It is San Marino's largest and most commercially oriented castello, taking in Dogana on the Italian frontier, where a busy road crossing, shops, transport links and steady tourist traffic give the district an everyday border-town, visitor-facing character. No municipal ordinance, local facility restriction, or recorded police or judicial practice in Serravalle governs how a trans visitor presents; the absence of published local data on the point, however, should not be read as reassurance. Social conditions are the more realistic concern: the district sits in a small, predominantly Catholic society where discretion is the norm and routine social curiosity is common, so conditional on being outed the exposure is social friction or bureaucratic confusion rather than official action. Reports of occasional anti-LGBTQ violence carry no published figures or local breakdown, so their frequency in Serravalle cannot be established. The area's settled, commercial and tourist-facing character may make a foreign gender-nonconforming visitor less conspicuous than in the smaller rural castelli, but this is a social impression rather than any documented protection.

regions.name: Banadir
regions.merged_summary: Banadir, centred on Mogadishu, is subject to Somalia's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is the most firmly under federal government administration in the country, and the insurgent territorial enforcement and judge-imposed capital punishment recorded elsewhere in Somalia do not operate locally; no documented local executions, protective mechanisms, trans community infrastructure or tolerance distinguish Banadir.
